p.seg: Nineteen Poems Presented to my Elder Brother, the Xiùcai Gōngmù, on His Entry into the Army
Nineteen Poems Presented to my Elder Brother, the Xiùcai Gōngmù, on His Entry into the Army
A pair of luán-phoenixes hide their brilliant radiance,
Furling their wings on the cliffs of Tàishān.
Raising their heads, they drink the morning dew,
Basking in the sun, they shake their feathered plumage.
With long cries, they frolic amidst the clouds,
At times descending to rest by the Orchid Pond.
They deem themselves free from the dust of the world,
Forever whole from beginning to end.
Who would have thought the world holds so many hardships?
The fowler comes and rouses my suspicion.
Cloud-nets block the four quarters,
High snares are set in jagged array.
Though they strive to fly, the situation is unfavorable,
Their great wing-feathers find no place to exert.
Hiding their grace, they submit to the long tether,
Finally becoming restrained by the times.
A lone male bird flies off in solitary departure,
His mournful song pained by the parting for life.
Lingering, he longs for his companion,
Resonant with grief on the slopes of the high mountain.
When the birds are gone, the good bow is put away;
When schemes reach their limit, the body must face peril.
Though good or ill fortune lies with oneself,
The paths of the world are full of steep dangers.
How can I return to my original robes,
Embracing jade and treasuring the six wonders?
Wandering at ease through the Great Clarity,
Hand in hand, following one another forever.
The mandarin ducks are flying,
Whirring go their wings.
In the morning they roam the high plains,
At evening they lodge on the orchid-islet.
Harmonious and clear is their singing,
Looking back and glancing at their mates,
Looking up and down with deep emotion,
Wandering at ease and leisurely.
The mandarin ducks are flying,
Calling their mates and summoning their companions.
In the morning they roam the high plains,
At evening they lodge on the central isle.
Necks intertwined, they shake their wings,
Drifting at ease in the clear current.
Chewing on orchids and iris,
Looking up and down, wandering at ease.
Swimming in that long river,
I rest upon its bank;
Climbing that high ridge,
I cut the thorn-shrubs there.
Alas, for my journeying and traveling,
Walking alone and solitary.
Looking up at that gentle Kǎifēng wind,
My tears fall like rain!
Swimming in that long river,
I rest upon its islet;
Climbing that high ridge,
I cut the wolfberries there.
Alas, for my solitary journey,
With no one to look to or rely upon.
Looking up at that gentle Kǎifēng wind,
Now I sit and now I rise.
The solemn and gentle breeze
Fans that light dust;
The shimmering white waves
Turn these swimming fish.
How great is my toil,
Having thoughts of a beautiful person.
Waking, I speak of long-lasting longing,
Truly concentrated on my close kin.
Where is my close kin?
Leaving me to travel far away.
Casting aside these fragrant sūn and zhǐ herbs,
To don those weeds of xiāo and ài.
Though the place be deep and secluded,
How could there be no falls and stumbles?
Thinking of the gentleman,
May harm not reach him from afar.
Human life is short of years,
But Heaven and Earth endure forever.
The term of a hundred years—
Who can call that a long life?
I long to ascend as an immortal,
To cross over into the imperishable.
Holding the reins, I hesitate,
Looking up and glancing at my friend.
Where is my friend going?
Separated by these mountain ridges.
Who says the River is wide?
A single reed can ferry across.
I only regret the eternal parting,
As he departs on that long road.
Gazing after him but unable to reach,
I pace back and forth in hesitation.
The fine horse is already well-trained,
The beautiful robes have a bright sheen.
On the left, I take up the Fánruò bow,
On the right, I receive the Wàngguī arrow.
Galloping like the wind and vanishing like lightning,
Treading on shadows and chasing flight.
Striking across the central plains,
Glancing around with spirited grace.
Taking my good companion with me,
Carrying me in a light carriage,
To the south, we cross the long hills,
To the north, we traverse the clear canals.
Above, I bring down the startled swan,
Below, I draw out the fish from the deep pool.
Whirling about in the hunt,
The joy is truly great.
Climbing high and gazing far,
Looking up and down, I sigh and lament.
Resenting that dark confinement,
Remote is the distant road.
Though there are fine melodies,
With whom can I sing pure songs?
Though there is a beautiful countenance,
For whom shall its splendor bloom?
I send a query to the high clouds,
I entrust my thoughts to the light waves.
Following the current to escape far away,
Holding my regrets in the mountain bend.
The light carriage travels swiftly,
Resting in that long forest.
The spring trees are in full bloom,
Spreading their leaves to cast a shade.
Gently blows the valley wind,
Brushing against my plain qín.
Chirp-chirp go the yellow birds,
Looking at their mates and playing with their songs.
Awakened and moved, my feelings race,
Thinking of the one I admire.
The sorrow in my heart—
I whistle and chant forever.
The vast and flooding stream
Girdles the borders of my state;
The lush green forest
Flourishes and radiates brilliance.
Fish and dragons splash about,
Mountain birds fly in flocks.
I go out for a journey in my carriage,
Until evening, forgetting to return.
Thinking of my good friend,
I am like one hungry and thirsty.
Wishing to speak but not succeeding,
How sorrowful and sad it is.
My followers rest in the orchid garden,
I fodder the horses at Huàshān.
Skipping stones on the level marshes,
Casting a line in the long river.
My eyes follow the returning swan,
My hand brushes the five strings.
Looking up and down, content with myself,
My mind wanders in the Great Mystery.
I praise that old fisherman,
Who got the fish and forgot the trap.
The man from Yǐng is gone,
Who can I speak to fully?
The quiet night is solemn and clear,
The bright moon shines on the balcony.
A slight breeze moves my skirt,
The braided curtains are pulled high.
Fine wine fills the goblet,
But there is no one with whom to share the joy.
The qín and sè are at hand,
But with whom can I play them?
I look up in admiration of one with the same path,
Whose fragrance is like the orchid.
Since the beautiful person is not here,
How can I not sigh forever!
Riding the wind to wander on high,
Climbing far up the Língqiū hill.
Entrusting my heart to Sōng Qiáo,
Hand in hand, we wander together.
At dawn, setting out from Tàihuà,
At evening, lodging in Shénzhōu.
Playing the qín and chanting poems,
For a while to forget my sorrows.
Finding joy in the qín and poetry,
Far wandering is to be cherished.
Embracing the Dào, I go forth alone,
Abandoning wisdom and forgetting the self.
Serene and without burden,
What should I seek from others?
Forever dwelling on the numinous peaks,
Delighting the will and nourishing the spirit.
Common customs are hard to awaken to,
following after things and never returning.
The perfect person looks far ahead,
returning to nature.
All things are as one,
the four seas are a single dwelling.
Sharing it with others,
what would I begrudge?
Life is like a floating sojourn,
briefly seen and suddenly ending.
Worldly affairs are numerous and chaotic,
I cast them aside for the most part.
Though the marsh pheasant is hungry,
it does not desire the garden forest.
How can one be harnessed and driven,
laboring the form and bittering the heart?
The body is precious and fame is lowly,
where do glory and disgrace lie?
What is precious is to follow one's will,
letting the heart go without regret.
One Poem of Profound Indignation
Alas, my meager fortune,
in youth I met with misfortune.
Mourning in loneliness with little knowledge,
I was yet in swaddling clothes.
My mother and elder brother raised me,
with kindness but without sternness.
Relying on love, I was willful and arrogant,
neither disciplined nor taught.
When I reached the age of adulthood,
relying on favor, I let myself go.
Uplifting my heart to hope for the ancients,
I indulged in what I valued.
Entrusting my interests to Lǎo and Zhuāng,
I slighted things and valued the self.
My will lay in guarding simplicity,
nourishing plainness and preserving the true.
I say that I am not clever,
loving the good but blind to people.
The defeat of Zǐyù,
repeatedly increased my faults.
The great man is inclusive and broad,
hiding filth and harboring shame.
People have many biases,
government is not of one's own making.
Only this narrow heart,
clearly distinguishes the good and the bad.
Awakened and thinking of my errors,
it is as painful as a wound.
Desiring to lessen my faults,
slander and criticism boiled over.
My nature does not harm things,
yet frequently draws resentment and hatred.
Formerly I felt ashamed before Liǔhuì,
now I am embarrassed before Sūn Dēng.
Internally I betray my long-held heart,
externally I am ashamed before my good friends.
Looking up in admiration to Yán and Zhèng,
rejoicing in the Way and living in leisure.
With the world I have no dealings,
my spirit and breath are peaceful and calm.
Alas that I am unfortunate,
entangled in troubles and many worries.
It did not descend from Heaven,
but truly resulted from my stubbornness and carelessness.
Reasoning failed and troubles knotted,
finally leading me to the dungeon.
Answering mean interrogations,
fettered in this dark obstruction.
Truly I am ashamed to plead my grievances,
the times are not with me.
Although I say my cause is upright,
my spirit is humiliated and my will is dejected.
Washing my body in the Cānglàng,
how can I say it can mend things?
The "yong-yong" calling of the migratory geese,
flapping their wings to travel north.
Moving according to the seasons,
attaining their desires and forgetting sorrow.
Alas, my indignant sighs,
none can ever compare.
Things go against my wishes,
encountering this long detention.
Failure and success are fated,
what else should I seek?
The ancients had a saying,
"In doing good, do not approach fame."
Serving the times with respect and silence,
blame and regret will not arise.
Wànshí was circumspect and cautious,
comforting his kin and preserving glory.
Worldly affairs are numerous and chaotic,
only disturbing my feelings.
In peace and joy one must be cautious,
then in the end there is perseverance.
The brilliant numinous Língzhī,
blooms three times in one year.
Why am I alone,
having a will that is not achieved?
Chastened by hardship, I think of returning,
my heart is pained within.
May I exert myself for the future,
with neither fragrance nor stench.
Gathering vetch on the mountain slope,
with loosened hair among the rocky peaks.
Forever whistling and long chanting,
nourishing my nature and cultivating longevity.
Two Poems Recounting My Will
The submerged dragon nurtures its divine form,
washing its scales and playing in the orchid pool.
Extending its neck, it yearns for Dàtíng,
resting its feet to await Huáng Xī.
The auspicious clouds have not yet cast their light,
it lingers on the slope of Cháoyáng.
The distant masses are not my peers,
who would be willing to correspond to worldly fitness?
Different kinds are hard to accommodate universally,
mean criticisms are numerous and scattered.
Obstructed and meeting with regret and stinginess,
my refined will cannot be exercised.
Plowing and weeding moved Nìng Yuè,
the horse's mat inspired Zhāng Yí.
I shall leave the group of companions,
leaning on a staff to follow Hóng Yá.
The Jiāopéng shakes its six pinions,
where can the fowler restrain it?
Floating and wandering in the Great Purity,
seeking anew for those who know me.
Flying wing-to-wing in the Yúnhàn,
drinking dew and eating the jasper branch.
Much I think of the people of the world,
harnessing their carriages early, they all gallop.
Quiet and still, one attains nature,
why bother with glory and splendor?
The quail is content in the wormwood forest,
looking up and laughing at the divine phoenix's flight.
The shallow well is the home of tadpoles and leeches,
where would the divine turtle return?
I regret being clumsy in managing myself,
following my will with many long thoughts.
Truly far removed and different from the world,
righteous reputation is not what I hope for.
Past events are already erroneous,
but what is to come can still be pursued.
Why be among human affairs,
making one's own heart unpeaceful?
Generously thinking of the ancients,
dreaming of seeing their countenances.
I wish to meet with one who knows me,
to vent my indignation and reveal the subtle.
In the mountain caves are many recluses,
rising lightly to seek my teacher.
In the morning climbing the peak of Jīshān,
until evening not knowing hunger.
Dwelling in the mystery, nourishing the soul,
for a thousand years forever at peace.
One Poem on Wandering Immortals
Gazing afar at the pines on the mountain,
the high ridges and valleys are lush and green.
How high they are naturally,
standing alone, distant and peerless.
I wish to wander beneath them,
but the paths are completely cut off.
Wáng Qiáo has left me and gone,
riding the clouds and driving six dragons.
Fluttering and playing in the Xuánpǔ,
meeting Huáng and Lǎo on the road.
They teach me the Way of Nature,
broad as if enlightening a child.
Gathering herbs at the corner of Zhōngshān,
ingesting them to change my appearance.
Like a cicada molting, I discard foul entanglements,
making friends and making a home at Bǎntóng.
Approaching the wine, playing the Jiǔsháo,
how harmonious the refined songs?
Long parted from the common people,
who can see my traces?
Ten Six-Word Poems
Ten Six-Word Poems
Only the ancient Yáo and Shùn,
the two had merits and virtues equal and even.
They did not treat the realm as a private family matter.
Noble, simple, kind, and yielding,
they brought peace and aid to the common people of the four seas.
In the age of Táng and Yú, the Way was governed,
the ten thousand states were harmonious and without affairs.
The worthy and the foolish each attained their will.
Peacefully at ease, internally forgetting themselves,
how beautiful that time, truly joyful.
When wisdom and cleverness are put to use, intentional action follows;
as laws and decrees become more prominent, bandits and thieves arise,
tangled and summoning one another without end.
The *Dàrén* is mysteriously silent and wordless;
he stabilizes the world with stillness so it rights itself.
Between fame and one's own person, which is more dear?
Alas, the common world sacrifices itself for glory!
They race and gallop, exhausting their strength and losing their essence.
Gains and losses are entangled in worry and alarm,
resulting in toil and a lack of peace.
Excessive concern for life invites calamity;
gold and jade filling a hall cannot be guarded.
The ancients were content with what was crude and plain,
taking only *Dào* and *Dé* as their friends;
thus they could extend their years and be immortal.
When fame and conduct are conspicuous, troubles increase;
high position and great power are the foundations of disaster.
Beautiful women sap the nature without doubt,
and rich flavors are a slow-acting poison hard to cure.
Why do greedy people not reflect on this?
Dōngfāng Shuò reached the heights of purity;
outwardly appearing corrupt, yet inwardly upright.
He soiled his body and used *gǔjī* humor to hide his name;
he was not entangled by the burdens of the world.
What he desired did not exceed his needs, so he did not strive.
Chǔ Zǐwén was good at serving;
thrice he became *Lìngyǐn* without joy.
Liǔxià Huì humbled himself and suffered disgrace,
yet did not treat rank or salary as his own.
In stillness and reverence, anciently there were only these two men.
Lǎo Lái’s wife had a virtuous name;
she did not wish for her husband to serve in Chǔ.
Together they avoided emolument and hid in farming,
delighting in the *Dào*, living in leisure, and gathering duckweed.
In the end, she maintained her high integrity without wavering.
Sigh at the ancient sage Yuán Xiàn,
who turned his back on fine food and a youthful face,
delighting in constant emptiness, hunger, and cold.
His form was shabby, but his body was at ease and his heart broad;
attaining his will, he lived his life without worry.
Seven Four-Character Poems Written Again, also titled *Qiū Hú Xíng*.
Seven Four-Character Poems Written Again.
Wealth, rank, and honor,
worries and troubles truly abound.
Wealth, rank, and honor,
worries and troubles truly abound.
What the ancients feared:
"A grand house casting a shadow over the family."
People harm those above them;
beasts detest the nets.
Only in poverty and low station
can one be free from other troubles.
I sing this to say:
Wealth and honor bring many worries.
Poverty and low station are easy to live in;
high success and grandeur are hard to maintain.
Poverty and low station are easy to live in;
high success and grandeur are hard to maintain.
To be ashamed of hearing direct speech
is to meet with disaster.
Changes and incidents are of ten thousand kinds,
turning good fortune into bad.
Longing to lead a yellow dog,
but that plan could not be followed.
I sing this to say:
High success and grandeur are hard to maintain.
Toil and humility lead to few regrets;
loyalty and trust bring long-lasting peace.
Toil and humility lead to few regrets;
loyalty and trust bring long-lasting peace.
The *Tiāndào* harms the full;
those who love to win are destroyed.
The forceful and violent invite disaster;
many affairs bring about trouble.
If you wish for peace and joy,
only be without fault.
I sing this to say:
Loyalty and trust bring long-lasting peace.
Those who overwork the spirit are exhausted;
extreme desires hasten withering.
Those who overwork the spirit are exhausted;
extreme desires hasten withering.
Yán Huí died young;
and even the young Tóng Wū.
Giving rein to the body in excess,
none fail to pass away early.
What kind of things are wine and sex?
Now they are no longer innocent.
I sing this to say:
Wine and sex cause one to wither.
Sever wisdom and discard learning;
let the mind wander in mysterious silence.
Sever sagehood and discard learning;
let the mind wander in mysterious silence.
If one meets with an error and regrets it,
then one should not be satisfied with oneself.
Dropping a fishing line in a single valley,
what one enjoys is a whole kingdom.
With loosened hair, walking and singing,
those who harmonize come from all directions.
I sing this to say:
Let the mind wander in mysterious silence.
I think of Wáng Qiáo,
riding the clouds and wandering the eight limits.
I think of Wáng Qiáo,
riding the clouds and wandering the eight limits.
Soaring over the *Wǔyuè*,
suddenly traveling ten thousand billions of miles.
Grant me the divine medicine,
and feathers and wings will grow of themselves.
Breathing the *Tàihé*,
refining the form and changing the complexion.
I sing this to say:
I think of wandering the eight limits.
Lingering about Zhōng Shān,
resting the carriage at the *Céngchéng*.
Lingering about Zhōng Shān,
resting the carriage at the *Céngchéng*.
Shaded by the *Huágài* above,
gathering the *Ruòyīng* blossoms below.
Receiving the *Dào* from the *Wáng Mǔ*,
then ascending to the Purple Court.
Roaming the heavenly pathways,
living for a thousand years.
I sing this to say:
Lingering at the *Céngchéng*.
A Poem Thinking of My Parents.
What can be done for this sorrow? The sorrow is unbearable.
Constantly aching, as if my heart were being drawn out.
What can be done for this sorrow? Sad thoughts are many.
My feelings are knotted and cannot be untangled.
Suddenly I have lost my mother’s protection and am left solitary,
mourning within myself until I lose my voice from weeping.
I wish to repay her virtue, but she is distantly gone.
Moved by her upbringing, my feelings are torn apart.
Alas, my mother and brother are forever hidden away.
Imagining their forms, I am devastated within.
Moved by the bright spring, I think of my compassionate mother;
I wish to see her once more, but there is no way.
Looking toward the *Nánshān*, I let out a mournful sigh.
Moved by the sight of her stool and staff, my tears flow like a stream.
Thinking of the past when my mother and brother were here,
my heart was at ease and joyful, as if living for an eternity.
Suddenly they have passed and cannot be pursued.
My heart is at its limit, filled only with grief.
I go up to the empty hall, which is vast and without support;
seeing their remaining possessions, my heart collapses.
In the middle of the night I am sad; to whom can I tell it?
Alone, I wipe away tears and harbor my sorrow.
As the days drift further away, my heart yearns;
longing for those who gave me life, I cannot stop my tears.
Now that my compassionate mother is gone, who will dote on me?
I look at myself with pity, my heart in distress.
I appeal to the blue heavens, but the heavens do not hear;
my tears fall like rain as I sigh to the blue clouds.
I wish to cast off my sorrow, but soon it returns;
the pain is deep and heavy, and cannot be restrained.
Three Poems in Response to the *èr Guō*.
People of the world are many and restless,
leaving the *Xiàjīng* to hurry to the *Shàngjīng*.
But you two *Guō* harbor a distinct spirit;
aloof and transcendent, you have come on a northern journey.
Delighting in the *Dào*, you entrust yourselves to a humble hut;
your elegant wills have nothing they strive for.
In this fine season, our wishes met,
and thus we formed a bond of joyful affection.
A gentleman stays close to what is righteous,
and our kindness and friendship have been sincere throughout our lives.
My own meager will has brought disaster upon itself,
repeatedly causing many conflicts to arise.
*Yù Zǐ* hid by the side of the bridge;
*Niè Zhèng* changed his appearance.
Considering this, I harbor fear and trepidation;
my concern is merely to find peace for myself.
Now I must stay in another land;
the prepared carriage cannot be stopped.
Originally I planned to finish our banquet and joy,
but now we can no longer be together.
You two have presented me with beautiful poems,
fragrant as the scent of hidden orchids.
Longing for the land and thinking of my dear ones,
how could my heart not be filled with indignation?
In the past, I inherited the legacy of my father and brother,
and in my youth, I was able to leave behind heavy burdens.
Due to my detachment, I eventually became lazy,
and I withdrew my tracks to the slopes of the northern mountains.
I only wished to nurture my nature and life,
and until the end of my days, have no other aim.
But auspicious times did not await me;
in my prime, I encountered a world of clamor and luxury.
In misfortune, I hurried toward the worldly teachings,
always fearing I would be caught in a net.
Fúxī and Shénnóng are already far and distant;
I beat my breast and sigh alone.
The admonition of Shù valued a yielding appearance;
the Fisherman liked to stir up waves.
Though escaping is also difficult,
it is not what my heart treasures.
Why not soar beyond the worldly realm,
eating jade and rinsing with morning mist?
Leaving things behind and discarding base burdens,
I wander freely in the Great Harmony.
I join friends at the spirit mountains,
playing the zither and singing pure songs.
If there is anyone who can follow this path,
why should the ancients be so highly praised?
Observing worldly affairs in detail,
difficulties and dangers bring much worry and anxiety.
Giving and receiving are traded like a market;
the Great Way is hidden and not extended.
On the level road, one encounters thorns and brambles;
where can one go even with peaceful steps?
Power and cunning struggle to overthrow each other;
fame and position are places one cannot dwell.
The luan and phoenix avoid the fowling nets;
they take refuge far away in the ruins of Kūnlún.
Zhuāng Zhōu grieved for the sacred tortoise;
Yuè Jì lamented for the royal carriage.
The Ultimate Person preserves it within himself,
hiding in simplicity and delighting in the dark void.
Why should fame and merit be worth dying for,
such that one wishes to be listed in the bamboo records?
If what one loves is truly like this,
then Yáng Zhū would sigh at the crossroads.
Go, go! Follow your own will;
I dare to decline if the paths do not go together.
A Poem for Ruǎn Dé-rú
A Poem for Ruǎn Dé-rú
Carrying grief, I return to my old hut;
moved deeply, my heart and liver are pained.
In a fine time, I met with you gentlemen;
our talk and consolation were as fragrant as orchids.
I regret that we did not meet sooner;
once face to face, it was like old joy.
I did not realize we would suddenly part forever;
thinking of the separation, I sigh in disappointment and sorrow.
There is nothing that does not happen in worldly affairs;
parting is easy, but meeting is truly difficult.
The man of Yǐng has suddenly passed away;
Carpenter Shí lies still and does not speak.
The marsh pheasant is confined to the wild grass;
the sacred tortoise delights in coiling in the mud.
Glorious name defiles a person's body;
high position brings many calamities and troubles.
It is better to cast off external burdens,
and give free rein to one's will to nurture the vast qi.
Yán Huí hoped to follow Yú Shùn;
Xízǐ admired Huáng Xuān;
who indeed were Juān and Péng?
They only placed their will where they felt at ease.
Gradually soaked and dying for immediate desires,
once gone, it is impossible to climb back.
Preserving life lies in prior accumulation;
do not console yourself with fear.
The southern land is dry and not cool;
plans for your attire should be completed early.
May you cherish your virtuous simplicity;
on the road, be careful of the wind and cold.
I exert myself to express what is in my heart;
as I face the writing, my feelings are bitter.
Seven Poems for a Wine Gathering
Seven Poems for a Wine Gathering
How joyful it is to wander in the garden,
surveying all around without end.
A hundred plants burst into fragrant bloom;
the lofty foundations stand tall and distant.
Forest trees are dense and intertwined;
in the dark pond, bream and carp play.
Light pellets fell the soaring birds;
fine lines pull out sturgeon and tuna.
Beautiful praise arises from those seated;
different temperaments share the same voice.
Beside the river, pure wine is offered;
subtle songs come from white teeth.
Plain zithers play elegant melodies;
clear sounds rise with the wind.
How could this gathering not be joyful?
I only regret the absence of Dōngyě-zǐ.
Amidst the wine, I think of the recluse,
who keeps to the old ways from beginning to end.
One should simply embody the seven strings,
and entrust the heart to a bosom friend.
Quietly, the flowing water
ripples and passes away;
Drifting, the cypress boat
now floats, now stays.
Softly whistling in the clear breeze,
drumming the oars at ease.
Letting go of the oars and casting the line,
wandering leisurely to the end of my years.
Graceful are those mandarin ducks,
folding their wings as they swim.
Bowing their heads to peck at green algae,
entrusting their bodies to the great flood.
In the morning, they fly over white rapids;
in the evening, they roost on spirit isles.
Swaying in the clear waves,
they sink and float along with them.
Water plants float in the Orchid Pond,
harmonious sounds are sharp and clear.
Playing the strings in the Qīngshāng mode,
the mind wanders in the Great Image.
Wholeheartedly devoted to cultivating the self,
the virtuous tones leave a lingering echo.
Zhōng Qī is no longer here;
who is there to appreciate my will?
Gathering the strings and dispersing thoughts,
wandering and fishing in the nine abysses.
Heavy currents are a thousand cubits deep,
where some bait is suspended.
How marvelous are Zhuāng and Lǎo,
who lived in retirement for many years.
Truly, it is a dragon-like transformation,
letting the will roam in the vastness.
Solemn is the cool wind,
arising by the river bank.
Turning my back on the Flowery Forest,
I look down at the Cinnabar Shore.
Containing yang and bursting with blossoms,
it does not wither even when treading on frost.
Alas, my view is different;
a hundred plants have all withered.
My heart is sorrowful;
who understands the dark mechanism?
Flourishing is the orchid fragrance,
growing in those central plains.
Green leaves are dark and lush;
beautiful buds are thick and numerous.
Fragrant, fragrant is the melilotus scent,
spreading with the wind.
It will enter the pepper chambers,
and emit its fragrance in the Dragon Pavilion.
Looking at those autumn grasses,
I am disappointed that they only wither.
One Miscellaneous Poem
A gentle breeze clearly fans;
clouds and mist are cleared away on all sides.
Bright, bright is the shining moon,
beautiful in the high corner.
I summon the young gentleman,
and we hold hands in the same carriage.
Dragon-steeds are majestic;
they toss their bits and hesitate.
Solemnly we journey through the night,
arriving at my friend's cottage.
Bright lamps emit their glow;
flowery curtains are draped long.
Luan-goblets pour out sweet wine;
divine cauldrons cook fish.
The strings surpass those of Zǐyě;
the singing exceeds that of Miánjū.
Chanting of the Great Simplicity,
we look down and praise the dark void.
Who can match the heroic and worthy?
I share the tally with you.
Rhapsody on the Zither, with Preface
I have been fond of music since I was young,
and as I grew older I continued to enjoy it.
I believe that while physical things have their cycles of prosperity and decay,
music remains unchanging;
one may grow weary of various flavors,
but of music one never tires.
For guiding and nourishing the spirit and vital energy,
and for giving expression to and harmonizing the emotions and will,
or for dwelling in poverty and solitude without feeling despondent,
nothing comes closer than music.
Therefore, even when repeating it is not enough,
one chants and sings to give free rein to the will;
when chanting and singing are not enough,
one entrusts words to expand the meaning.
However, concerning the instruments of the eight sounds
and the forms of song and dance,
talented scholars of successive generations have composed rhapsodies for them.
In praising their structure and form,
their styles and traditions invariably follow one another;
in describing their materials,
they regard hardship and distress as superior;
in rhapsodizing their sounds,
they take sorrow and lamentation as primary;
in admiring their transformative influence,
they value the shedding of tears.
Though beautiful they may be,
they have not fully grasped the underlying principles.
Tracing the source of their views,
it seems they fundamentally do not understand music;
looking at their objectives,
they also fail to reach the true essence of ritual and music.
Among the various instruments,
the virtue of the *qín* is most excellent.
Therefore, I have recorded my thoughts
to compose this rhapsody.
The text says:
Consider where the *yǐ* and *wú* trees are born,
they rely on the lofty ridges of high peaks.
Cleaving through layers of soil, they are born and carried forth;
they reach toward the *Chénjí* and soar high.
They contain the pure harmony of Heaven and Earth,
and absorb the glorious light of the sun and moon.
Lush and dense, they flourish alone,
spreading their flowery blossoms into the *Hàocāng*.
In the evening, they receive the shadows from the *Yúyuān*;
in the morning, they dry their trunks in the *Jiǔyáng*.
Passing through a thousand years to wait for their value,
they stand in silent divinity, eternally at peace.
Moreover, the terrain of the mountains and rivers
is winding, secluded, and deep,
with towering, jagged peaks.
Interlocking ridges are steep and rocky,
with craggy heights and precipitous slopes.
Cinnabar cliffs are dangerous and narrow,
and green walls reach up ten thousand fathoms.
When layered peaks rise even higher,
they loom grandly, covered by clouds.
Distant and exalted, they are extremely magnificent,
rising loftily and uniquely elegant.
They steam with spiritual fluids to scatter clouds,
and based on divine abysses, they pour forth streams.
Then, the surging waves rush and collide,
madly racing and competing to flow.
Striking rocks and hitting bends,
they are pent up with anger, then majestic and grand.
Billowing and surging, they toss and strike,
whipping up foam and raising waves.
Gushing and splashing with a roar,
they coil and entwine like snakes.
They run wild into the great rivers,
crossing through the *Zhōngzhōu*.
Then peacefully turning and slowly moving,
they float silently and far away.
Tranquil and vast,
they encircle and embrace the hills.
Observe closely the products of its soil,
and the treasures cultivated in its mysterious spaces.
Rare and strange are the *lánggān* gems,
and the *yáojǐn* jades are bright and radiant.
Clustered and piled up,
they spread brilliantly at its side.
Spring orchids cover its eastern side,
while *shātáng* trees grow in the west.
*Juānzǐ* dwells on its sunny southern slope,
and jade-like wine springs forth before it.
Dark clouds provide shade above,
and soaring phoenixes gather at its peak.
Pure dew moistens its bark,
and a gentle breeze flows through it.
Upright and solemn in its quietude,
dense and subtle in its tranquil leisure.
That which surrounds it
is indeed naturally divine and beautiful,
sufficient to inspire longing and love.
Thus, those who have withdrawn from the world,
the likes of *Róng Qī* and the *Qǐ Jì* group,
together they ascend the flying bridge
and cross the secluded ravines.
Grasping jade-like branches,
climbing steep cliffs,
they wander beneath it.
Looking around and gazing afar,
they feel as though they are soaring.
They glance sideways at *Kūnlún*,
and look down at the edge of the sea.
They point to the distant *Cāngwú*,
and face the meandering curves of the *Huíjiāng*.
Realizing the many burdens of worldly customs,
they look up to the lingering brilliance of *Jīshān*.
Admiring the vastness of this peak,
their hearts are stirred, and they forget to return.
With emotions relaxed and gaze wide,
they encounter the legacy of *Xuānyuán*.
Longing for *Lǎotóng* at the corner of *Guī*,
they admire the high chanting of *Tàiróng*.
Looking at this *wú* tree, thoughts arise,
thinking to use this object to entrust the heart.
They then cut a branch
and measure it for its purpose;
the perfect man expresses his thoughts
and crafts it into an elegant *qín*.
They have *Lízǐ* supervise the ink-marking
and *Jiàng Shí* wield the axe;
*Kuí* and *Xiāng* recommend the methods,
and *Bān* and *Chuí* exert their divine skill.
Engraving the joints and fitting the pieces,
clear and dense, the tuning is balanced.
Ornately painted and carved,
displaying patterns and hanging designs.
Inlaid with rhino horn and ivory,
lined with kingfisher green.
Strung with the silk of *Yuánkè*,
and with studs of jade from *Zhōngshān*.
There are images of dragons and phoenixes,
and the forms of ancient men:
*Bó Yá* waving his hands,
and *Zhōng Qī* listening to the sounds.
Their radiant appearances are dazzling,
emitting brilliance and spreading light.
How beautiful it is!
*Líng Lún* tunes the pitch-pipes,
and *Tián Lián* handles the strings.
Presented to the gentleman,
the new sounds are clear and bright.
How magnificent it is!
When first tuned,
then *jué* and *yǔ* notes rise together,
and *gōng* and *zhǐ* notes confirm each other.
Diverse notes break out and race together,
high and low notes respond in layers,
skipping and leaping,
beautiful sounds are about to arise.
It is already harmonious and smooth, enough to be enjoyed.
Then, the proper sounds are regulated,
and wondrous melodies are played;
performing *Báixuě*,
and sounding the *Qīngjué*.
Plentiful and overflowing, they drift away,
brilliantly spreading and richly abundant.
Radiant and shining, they soar high,
racing urgently in succession.
Copiously surging and meeting, they compete to race,
gathering together in glorious and intricate patterns.
Their form is like towering mountains,
and again like flowing waves,
vast and surging,
dense and lofty.
Agitated and troubled,
winding and dancing.
Rising and letting loose, scattering and escaping,
sudden and flowing like blossoming flowers.
Maintaining the appearance and following the rhythm,
responding to changes with the proper measure.
Striving for fame and excelling in their craft,
keeping to the track with steady steps.
Vast and gentle,
the fame of the sound spreads far.
Containing manifest charm to the very end,
the lingering echoes drift into the *Tàisù*.
In high carriages and soaring pavilions,
or in wide halls and quiet rooms,
on a solemn and clear winter night,
when the bright moon sheds its light.
New robes are bright and colorful,
and the tassels and studs emit fragrance.
Thereupon the instrument is cool and the strings are tuned;
the heart is at ease and the hands are agile.
Plucking and striking as one desires;
following only where the intent suggests.
First venturing into *Lù Shuǐ*;
then playing the *Qīng Zhǐ* mode.
Elegantly expanding on *Táng Yáo*;
finally chanting of *Wēi Zǐ*.
Broad, clear, grand, and moist;
leisurely wandering and pausing.
Strumming the strings and singing calmly;
new sounds arise in succession.
The song says:
"Soaring on the *Fú Yáo* whirlwind to rest at *Yíng Zhōu*;
inviting *Liè Zǐ* to be a good companion.
Feasting on the *Hàng Xiè* mist and wearing the morning clouds;
fluttering distantly to roam the edge of heaven.
Equalizing all things and transcending in self-contentment;
entrusting life and fate to go or stay as they will.
Stirring clear echoes to join the gathering;
how intimate is the union of strings and song!"
Thereupon, as the melody draws to a close;
and the various sounds are about to cease.
Changing the rhythm and altering the key;
a marvelous improvisation then breaks forth.
Lifting a harmonious countenance;
baring the white wrists.
Slender fingers fly and race along;
sounds bustle and chatter in a flowing flood.
Sometimes lingering in fond remembrance;
pent up, suppressed, and pressed down.
Revolving and nurturing;
leisurely and privately enjoying.
Suddenly breaking free with vigorous spirit;
like winds startling and clouds in chaos.
Scattered and fierce;
spreading out and half dispersing.
Abundant and blending, then splitting apart;
elegant, brilliant, and magnificent.
Heroic sounds burst forth and soar;
vibrant and resplendent.
Sometimes intermittent sounds intermingle;
appearing like strange pursuits.
Two beauties advance together;
like horses galloping side by side or wings driving forward.
At first appearing as if about to diverge;
but in the end following the same path.
Sometimes winding but not bent;
straight but not arrogant.
Sometimes overlapping without confusion;
sometimes separating without becoming distinct.
Occasionally sudden and forceful with high spirits;
or resentful and harsh, yet hesitating.
Suddenly drifting and moving lightly;
then briefly lingering and branching out.
Sometimes uneven and hurried;
layered and crowded together.
Crisscrossing in continuous succession;
fleeing and pursuing, pressing upon each other.
Sighs of admiration and repeated praise;
without a moment’s breath in between.
Rare, beautiful, wondrous, and grand;
so exhaustive they cannot be fully known.
As for the relaxed, leisurely, and refined parts;
the loud and the soft are each appropriate.
Clear, harmonious, orderly, and expansive;
undulating and multifaceted.
Solemn and gentle to delight the heart;
yielding and orderly, moving with ease.
Sometimes taking risks to find the convergence;
seeking openings and rushing into danger.
Resonating like a lone *kūn* bird crying by a clear pond;
winging like a floating swan soaring over high cliffs.
Tangled patterns and trailing elegance;
silken banners fluttering and spreading out.
A gentle breeze and lingering notes;
delicate and graceful.
Sometimes dragging, striking, scraping, or stroking;
swirling, flowing, and pure.
Lightly moving and floating plucks;
bright, beautiful, and clever.
Rapid but not hurried;
lingering but not stagnant.
Fluttering and drifting far away;
faint notes quickly vanishing.
Listening from afar;
it is like *luán* and *fèng* phoenixes singing in harmony, playing amidst the clouds.
Observing from nearby;
it is like a multitude of flowers blooming in glory, shining in the spring breeze.
Not only abundant and full of variety;
but also beginning well and ending beautifully.
Ah, how exquisite and grandly beautiful;
how infinite are its transformations!
When the three months of spring begin;
and beautiful garments are worn according to the season.
One then takes hold of friends;
to invite them and to enjoy oneself.
Walking through orchid gardens;
climbing onto tiered terraces.
With long forests at one's back;
shaded by flowery canopies.
Overlooking clear streams;
composing new poems.
Praising the leisurely joy of fish and dragons;
delighting in the flourishing growth of a hundred plants.
Performing the legacy melodies of *Chóng Huá*;
feeling moved by distant admiration and long thoughts.
Or in a magnificent hall at a private banquet;
with close friends and nearby guests.
Fragrant delicacies are served together;
delicious wine is clear and pure.
Presenting the music of *Nán Jīng*;
sounding the tunes of *Xī Qín*.
Continuing with *Líng Yáng*;
performing the melodies of *Bā Rén*.
Variations are mixed and arise together;
startling the audience and amazing the spirit.
Evaluating the exceptional merit and comparing the performances;
how could the mouth-organ or the flute ever be its equal?
If one lists the appropriate melodies and preludes;
then there are *Guǎng Líng Zhǐ Xī*;
*Dōng Wǔ* and *Tài Shān*;
*Fēi Lóng* and *Lù Míng*;
*Kūn Jī* and *Yóu Xián*.
They alternate in singing and playing;
the sounds seem natural.
Flowing with the elegance of *Chǔ*;
checking impetuousness and washing away vexation.
Descending to the popular ballads;
the five pieces of the *Cài Shì* family.
*Wáng Zhāo* and *Chǔ Fēi*;
*Qiān Lǐ Bié Hè*.
There are still some others;
to be played in intervals or when nothing else is available;
there are also things worth observing there.
However, if one is not a person of broad and far-reaching mind;
one cannot roam and play with it.
If one is not a person of deep stillness;
one cannot dwell in leisure with it.
If one is not a person of unrestrained transcendence;
one cannot be without regret with it.
If one is not a person of the utmost refinement;
one cannot analyze its principles with it.
If one discusses its form and structure;
and examines its character and sound:
the instrument is harmonious, so the echoes are carefree;
the tension is tight, so the sounds are clear;
the intervals are wide, so the tones are low;
the strings are long, so the bridge positions resonate.
Its nature is pure and quiet to straighten the principles;
it contains the harmony of the highest virtue.
Truly it can move and stir the heart's intent;
and release hidden emotions.
Therefore, when those harboring grief hear it;
none are not filled with trembling sorrow;
dejected and heartbroken.
Harboring sorrow and groaning in distress;
they cannot restrain themselves.
When those who are healthy and happy hear it;
then they are delighted and joyful;
clapping, dancing, and brimming with excitement.
Lingering and overflowing;
laughing and chuckling all day long.
If those who are balanced and peaceful listen to it;
then they are nourished and pleased;
virtuous, solemn, and mysteriously true.
Calm and empty, delighting in antiquity;
forsaking affairs and forgetting the self.
Thus *Bó Yí* used it to be incorruptible;
*Yán Huí* used it to be humane;
*Bǐ Gān* used it to be loyal;
*Wěi Shēng* used it to be trustworthy;
*Huì Shī* used it to be eloquent;
*Wàn Shí* used it to be slow of speech and cautious.
Others extended this to similar categories;
the effects were not just one;
they returned to the same end by different paths;
some ornate and some plain.
Summarizing central harmony to govern all things;
all using it daily without fail.
Its power to move people and things;
is truly grand indeed.
At that time,
metal and stone instruments fell silent,
and gourd and bamboo instruments held their breath.
Wáng Bào ceased his singing,
and Dí Yá lost his sense of taste.
Tiān Wú leaped within the deep abyss,
and Wáng Qiáo parted the clouds and descended.
The Yuèzhuó danced upon the courtyard steps,
and wandering goddesses floated down to gather there.
It moved Heaven and Earth to bring about harmony;
how much more so the various crawling creatures.
I admire the excellent luxuriance of this instrument,
and chant this composition to comfort myself.
Ever to use and wear it without weariness,
it is truly what has been prized from antiquity to the present.
The Envoi says:
The peaceful and deep virtue of the qín,
is beyond measure!
With a pure substance and a distant mind,
it is remote and difficult to reach!
Fine quality and beautiful hands
meet in this present age!
In a profusion of harmonious sounds,
it crowns all the various arts!
Those who understand its sound are rare;
who can truly treasure it?
The one who can fully realize the elegant qín
is only the Perfected Person!
A Letter to Shān Jùyuán Breaking off Friendship.
Kāng declares:
You formerly praised me in Yǐngchuān,
and I have always called these the words of one who knows me.
However, I have occasionally wondered about this sentiment;
as I was not yet intimately familiar with you,
how did you come to understand it so quickly?
Returning from Hédōng the year before last,
Xiǎn Zōng and Ā Dū mentioned that you proposed that I should replace you in office.
Though the matter did not proceed,
I know now that you do not, after all, truly know me.
You are versatile and broad-minded,
finding many things acceptable and few things strange.
My nature is upright and my mind is narrow;
there is much I cannot endure,
and it was only by chance that we became friends.
Recently I heard of your promotion,
and I felt a start of displeasure.
I feared that you, ashamed of the cook carving alone,
might drag in the priest to help him;
with your own hand offering the phoenix-handled knife,
only to smear it with the rank smell of raw meat.
Therefore, I shall explain in detail for you what is and is not possible for me.
In the past, when I read books,
I encountered men of unyielding integrity;
some said such people did not exist,
but now I believe they truly do.
If one's nature cannot endure something,
it truly cannot be forced.
Now, it is common talk that enlightened men find nothing they cannot endure,
outwardly not different from the common folk,
yet inwardly not losing their integrity;
following the current of their generation,
without giving rise to regret or shame.
Lǎozǐ and Zhuāng Zhōu
are my teachers,
and they personally held humble posts.
Liǔxià Huì and Dōngfāng Shuò
were enlightened men,
who were at peace in low positions.
How would I dare to disparage them?
Furthermore, Zhòngní loved all,
not ashamed to be a whip-holder,
and Zǐwén had no desire for high ministerial office,
yet thrice became Lìngyǐn;
this is the intention of a gentleman to help the world.
As it is said, when successful, they can benefit all without changing,
and when in straits, they are content and free from distress.
Looking at it this way,
Yáo and Shùn's ruling of the world,
Xǔ Yóu's dwelling in the cliffs,
Zǐfáng's assisting Hàn,
and Jièyú's singing as he walked,
were all of the same principle.
Looking up at these several gentlemen,
they can be called those who were able to fulfill their own wills.
Thus, though a gentleman has a hundred ways of acting,
they follow different paths to the same destination.
Acting in accordance with one's nature,
each attaches themselves to what they find peaceful.
Thus there are the discussions of "Staying in court and not leaving"
and "Entering the mountains and forests and not returning."
Moreover, the man of Yánlíng praised the character of Zǐzāng,
and Chángqīng admired the integrity of Xiàngrú.
Where one's will and spirit reside,
cannot be taken away.
Every time I read the biographies of Shàng Zipíng and Tái Xiàowēi,
I am moved to admire them,
and I imagine the kind of people they were.
Left orphaned and exposed in my youth,
I was spoiled by my mother and elder brother,
and did not study the Classics.
By nature I am also careless and lazy,
my muscles are weak and my flesh is soft.
I often go fifteen days or a month without washing my head or face.
Unless it is very itchy or uncomfortable,
I cannot bring myself to bathe.
Often when I need to urinate, I endure it and do not get up,
waiting until my bladder is about to burst before I finally rise.
Furthermore, I have been unconstrained and idle for a long time,
my disposition is proud and scattered,
my lack of restraint goes against ritual,
and laziness and arrogance reinforce each other.
Yet I have been treated with indulgence by my peers,
who do not attack my faults.
Furthermore, reading Zhuāng and Lǎo
has further increased my unrestrained ways,
thus causing any ambition for glory and progress to decline daily,
while my desire to follow my true nature becomes firmer.
This is like a wild bird or deer; if domesticated while young,
it will obey training and rules;
but if captured when grown,
it will look wildly about and tug at its tether,
even if it means leaping into boiling water or fire.
Though adorned with a golden bit,
and fed with fine delicacies,
it only longs more for the deep forests,
and its will remains in the tall grass.
Ruǎn Sìzōng never spoke of others' faults,
and I always try to emulate him,
but have not been able to achieve it.
He was superior in his innate nature,
doing no harm to others,
only his drinking was excessive.
Yet he was restrained by the followers of ritual and law,
who hated him like an enemy,
and it was only thanks to the Dàjiāngjūn protecting him that he survived.
I am not as worthy as Sìzōng,
and I have the flaws of arrogance and laxity.
Moreover, I do not understand human nature
and am ignorant of the opportune moment,
lacking the prudence of Wànshí
while having the burden of liking to speak my mind fully.
If I were in contact with affairs for long,
faults and conflicts would arise daily.
Even if I wished to avoid trouble,
could it be possible?
Furthermore, human relations have rituals
and the court has laws;
I have considered this very thoroughly,
and there are seven things I certainly cannot endure,
and two things that are strictly impossible.
I like to sleep and wake up late,
but the gatekeeper would call me incessantly;
this is the first thing I cannot endure.
Carrying my lute and singing while I walk,
hunting and fishing in the wilds,
yet having officials and soldiers guarding me,
unable to move freely;
this is the second thing I cannot endure.
Sitting upright for a long time,
my legs becoming numb and unable to move,
and by nature having many lice,
scratching myself without end;
yet I would have to be wrapped in official robes,
bowing and saluting superior officers;
this is the third thing I cannot endure.
I have never been good at writing letters,
nor do I enjoy writing them;
yet in the human world there are many affairs,
piling up on the desk and filling the table.
If I do not respond,
it would violate social teaching and harm righteousness;
if I try to force myself,
I cannot sustain it for long.
This is the fourth thing I cannot endure.
I do not like attending funerals,
yet the human way considers this important.
I have already been resented by those who do not forgive,
even to the point of those who wish to slander me.
Though I might startle and blame myself,
my nature cannot be transformed.
To lower my heart and follow the crowd
would be deceitful and insincere,
and in the end I still could not avoid blame.
Being without praise like this;
this is the fifth thing I cannot endure.
I do not like vulgar people,
yet I would have to work together with them.
Or guests would fill the seats,
their clamor deafening my ears.
In the midst of noise, dust, and stench,
a thousand changes and a hundred tricks
unfolding before one's eyes.
This is the sixth thing I cannot endure.
My heart is impatient with troublesome matters,
yet official business is overwhelming.
Administrative affairs would entangle my heart,
and worldly concerns would multiply my worries.
This is the seventh thing I cannot endure.
Furthermore, I often criticize Tāng and Wǔ,
and disparage Zhōu and Kǒng;
in the human world, one cannot stop at this,
it will surely be evident that I am not tolerated by the teachings of the world;
this is the first thing that is strictly impossible.
Being of a rigid temperament and hating evil,
I speak my mind freely and carelessly,
speaking out whenever I encounter something;
this is the second thing that is strictly impossible.
With a nature that is narrow-minded and cautious,
governed by these nine troubles,
if there is no external calamity,
there will surely be internal illness;
how could I remain for long in the human world?
Moreover, I have heard the bequeathed words of Taoist masters
that consuming Shù and Huángjīng
gives a person longevity.
I believe this deeply.
Wandering in the mountains and marshes,
observing the fish and birds,
my heart takes great joy in this;
but once I become an official,
these things will be abandoned.
How can I abandon what I enjoy
and follow what I fear?
Now, when people know each other,
they value understanding each other's innate nature
and thus helping them fulfill it.
Yǔ did not coerce Bóchéng Zǐ,
thus fully preserving his integrity;
Zhòngní did not borrow a carriage-cover from Zǐxià,
to protect their shortcomings.
In recent times, Zhūgě Kǒngmíng did not pressure Yuánzhí to enter the state of Shǔ,
and Huà Zǐyú did not compel Yòu'ān to take the position of a high minister.
This can be called being able to maintain a relationship from beginning to end,
and being those who truly know one another.
You see that straight wood cannot be made into a wheel,
and curved wood cannot be made into a rafter;
this is because one does not wish to twist their natural talent,
but rather lets each find its proper place.
Therefore, the four classes of people have their respective occupations,
and each finds joy in fulfilling their own aspirations.
Only a man of broad understanding can facilitate this;
this should be within your consideration.
One cannot, simply because they themselves like the Zhāngfǔ cap,
force the people of Yuè to wear a formal crown.
Or, because one craves rotten meat,
feed a young yuānyāng bird with a dead rat.
I have lately been studying the art of nourishing life,
distancing myself from external glory,
abandoning rich flavors,
letting my mind wander in silence,
and valuing non-action.
Even if I did not have the nine difficulties,
I would still not care for what you enjoy;
furthermore, I have an ailment of chest congestion,
which has recently become more severe.
Testing myself in private,
I find I cannot endure what I do not enjoy.
I have examined my own fate clearly.
If the way ends and the road is exhausted,
then so be it.
You should not needlessly wrong me
and cause me to roll into a ditch.
I have recently lost the joy of my mother and elder brother,
and my mind is often sorrowful.
My daughter is thirteen,
and my son is eight;
they have not yet reached adulthood,
and moreover, they are often ill.
Looking at them with such regret,
how can words express it?
Now I only wish to stay in my humble lane,
teach and raise my children and grandchildren,
occasionally reminisce with old relatives and friends,
and talk about our lives.
A cup of cloudy wine,
a tune on the qín,
and my wishes are fulfilled.
If you persist in pestering me,
it is merely because you wish to find a man for the government
to benefit the needs of the times.
You have long known that I am eccentric and careless,
and not attuned to worldly affairs;
I myself also realize I am not as virtuous or capable as today's men.
If you think common people all love glory
and that only I can leave it behind and find joy in doing so,
this is the closest thing that can be said.
But only if one has great talent and broad capacity,
mastering everything,
yet remaining uncalculating,
is it truly noble.
If I, being sickly,
wish to leave affairs to preserve myself
and protect my remaining years,
this is truly due to my deficiencies;
how can one see a eunuch and call him chaste?
If you simply wish to climb the royal road together,
hoping to bring me along
for occasional mutual joy,
once you pressure me,
it will surely trigger my madness.
Unless there were a deep grudge,
it would not come to this.
There was a rustic man who enjoyed warming his back in the sun and eating celery,
and wished to offer these to the Emperor;
though his intentions were sincere,
they were ill-conceived.
I hope you will not be like him.
My intentions are thus;
I have explained them to you,
and also to bid farewell.
Jī Kāng speaks.
One Letter Breaking off Friendship with Lǚ Chángtì
Kāng speaks:
In the past, since our ages were comparable,
we often met and were close.
Your sincere intentions
led to a great friendship.
Thus I regarded you as a most intimate friend.
Although our paths of service and retirement differed,
our affection did not decline.
Later, I came to know your younger brother Ādū,
whose will and strength were enlightened.
I was always happy that your family had such a brother.
But last year, Ādū spoke to me;
he was truly indignant about your intention to report him.
I deeply suppressed his anger,
and relying on my belief that you would not pressure him,
he followed my advice.
In the meantime, I told you
that because he followed me,
you should be harmonious with your kin.
This was to protect your family's gate
and to keep both sides safe.
Furthermore, you promised me you would never attack Ādū,
swearing it by the friendship between father and son.
I was deeply moved by your heavy words,
comforted and explained this to Ādū,
and Ādū was then relieved.
He no longer held intentions against you,
yet you secretly harbored doubts,
covertly memorialized to attack Ādū,
and were the first to confess and falsely accuse him.
Because of Ādū,
you trusted me yet said nothing.
How could I have known you concealed such a treacherous heart?
That Ādū tolerated you
was truly because of my words.
Now that Ādū has been charged with a crime,
I have failed him.
My failing Ādū
is due to your failing me.
Dejected and having lost my way,
what more is there to say!
Under such circumstances,
I have no heart to associate with you anymore.
The gentlemen of old did not utter ugly words when breaking off a friendship.
From here we part!
Feeling deep resentment at this parting.
Jī Kāng speaks.
One scroll of Bǔ Yí Jí
One scroll of Bǔ Yí Jí
There was a Hóngdá Xiānshēng:
vast and broad was his magnanimity,
serene, detached, and expansive.
He was upright but not restrictive,
sharp-edged but not harmful.
He walked alone, transcending the world,
carrying jade while wearing coarse hemp.
In his associations, he did not improperly conform;
in service, he did not seek high attainment.
He always believed that loyalty, trustworthiness, sincerity, and respect,
when practiced on a straight path,
would allow one to live among the Jiǔyí,
travel through the Bāmán,
float upon the Cānghǎi,
and tread the source of the Hé.
Armored soldiers were not worth fearing,
and fierce beasts were not a concern.
Therefore, calculating motives did not exist in him;
he was placid and purely simple.
He was at ease and unrestrained,
forgetting likes and dislikes.
Taking the Tiāndào as his single guide,
he took no notice of the trivial affairs of the myriad things.
However, since the Dàdào has been hidden,
cleverness and artifice have flourished;
worldly customs have become sticky and complicated,
and human sentiments have grown multifaceted.
Wherever profit lies,
it is as if birds were chasing a luán.
Wealth becomes a gathering of moths,
nobility a collection of resentments;
those who act suffer many burdens,
while those who stay still have few troubles.
Thus, he thought of the hermits in the hills,
and the joy of those holding fishing rods by the rivers.
Thereupon, in far-reaching reflection and long contemplation,
he became transcendent and lost in thought.
Since the man of Yǐng has passed away,
who shall be my sounding board?
Since I cannot meet a sage,
I hope to hear of it through the arts of divination.
So he went to the cottage of Tàishǐ Zhēnfù
and visited him, saying:
"I have certain doubts;
I wish for you to divine them."
Zhēnfù then sat upright and handled the milfoil stalks,
dusted the table and laid out the tortoise shell, saying:
"What are your instructions?"
The Gentleman said:
"Should I rouse my indignation and display my sincerity,
speaking uprightly in the imperial court,
without bowing to kings and dukes?
Or should I be humble, weak, and compliant,
following orders and swaying with others,
practicing outward obedience?
Should I be gentle, kind, and broadly protective,
bestowing favors without expecting gratitude?
Or should I pursue worldly profit,
improperly seeking acceptance and illicitly conforming?
Should I live in seclusion and practice righteousness,
extending perfect sincerity, or should I exalt adornment and engage in deceit,
cultivating a hollow reputation?
Should I cast out the wicked and treacherous,
maintaining integrity without wavering,
and distinguishing between the bad and the good?
Or should I be arrogant and glib,
using cleverness and relying on tactics,
to become a 'bag of wisdom'?
Should I be a companion to Wáng Qiáo and Chì Sōng?
Or should I promote Yī Zhì
and take Shàngfù as a friend?
Should I hide my scales and conceal my colors,
like a dragon in the deep?
Or should I spread my wings and raise my voice,
like a wild swan among the clouds?
Should I outwardly transform my appearance,
and inwardly hide my feelings,
bending my body to follow the times
and sinking into the world without a name;
so that though I am among men,
I truly dwell in the darkness?
Or should I be impassioned for the sake of purity
and sharpen my thoughts for the sake of essence,
with actions different from the world
but a heart aligned with the common folk;
so that wherever I am, I must be heard, constantly bustling about?
Should I be solitary, detached, and free,
with nothing to boast of or admire;
making 'that' and 'I' as one,
neither competing nor yielding;
letting my mind wander in the bright and pure,
and suddenly entering a state of 'sitting in oblivion';
chasing after Xī and Nóng but failing to catch up,
and feeling melancholy while on the path?
Or should I be fervent and consider it magnanimous,
expressing deep emotion as brilliance;
above, challenging the lord of ten thousand chariots,
below, insulting generals and ministers;
making my countenance dignified and stern,
loftily acting with defiance;
always acting as if I have lost my position,
and harboring resentment in dissatisfaction?
Should I accumulate goods worth billions,
dining to the sound of bells and with tripod-vessels;
reclining on fragrances,
and being charmed by beautiful women?
Or should I toil my body and exhaust my strength,
clearing away thorns and brambles;
living in the mountains and drinking from the valleys,
resting against the cliffs?
Should I be like Bófèn and Zhòngkān,
making the 'two eights' my peers;
expelling Gòng and Gǔn,
causing them to lose their places?
Or should I be like the man of Jīshān
or the father of Yǐngshuǐ;
treating Táng and Yú with contempt,
and laughing at Dà Yǔ?
Should I be like Tàibó's hidden virtue,
yielding in secret without making it known?
Or should I be like Jì Zhá's conspicuous integrity and righteousness,
aspiring to be like Zǐzāng?
Should I be like Lǎo Dān's purity, stillness, and subtlety,
guarding the mystery and embracing the One?
Or should I be like Zhuāng Zhōu's leveling of things and transformation,
penetratingly thorough and unrestrained?
Should I be like Yíwú, who did not begrudge his shackles,
and ultimately established his achievement as a hegemon?
Or should I be like Lǔ Lián, who treated the world lightly and gave free rein to his will,
talking loftily and acting at ease?
Should I be like Shìnánzǐ's spiritual courage and internal firmness,
with a will as steady as mountains and deep as chasms?
Or should I be like Máogōng and Lìnshēng, with the stride of a dragon and the step of a tiger,
aspiring to be a heroic man?
Among these, who gained and who lost?
What is ill-fortune and what is auspicious?
Times have shifted and customs have changed,
people love nobility and admire fame;
Zāng Wén would not yield his position to Liǔ Jì,
and Gōngsūn would not attribute beauty to Dǒng Shēng;
once Jiǎ Yì met an enlightened ruler,
Jiàng and Guàn changed their expressions and raised their voices.
How much more so now, when a thousand dragons race together,
and ten thousand steeds go forth;
in a chaotic scramble,
passing like shooting stars.
How could I dare not seek counsel from one so experienced?"
Tàishǐ Zhēnfù said:
"I have heard that the Perfect Man does not look at physiognomy,
and the Attained Man does not divine.
As for a gentleman like you,
culture and enlightenment reside within;
you manifest simplicity and embrace the uncarved block.
Inwardly, you have no shame in your heart;
outwardly, you do not fail the world.
Your friendships are not for profit;
your service is not for salary.
You reflect upon the past and present,
cleansing your emotions and sweeping away desires.
In such a state,
you can swim in Lǚliáng,
and you can bathe in Tānggǔ;
you are about to watch the Dàpéng at the Nánmíng,
so what worry have you for the petty grievances of the human world!"
One Piece of the "Discourse on Nourishing Life."
In the world, there are those who say that divine immortals can be achieved through learning,
and that immortality can be attained through effort.
Others say that the maximum lifespan is one hundred and twenty years,
which has been the same throughout ancient and modern times;
and that anything beyond this,
is nothing but demonic delusion.
Both of these views miss the true nature of the matter.
Let me attempt a brief discussion of it.
Now, although divine immortals are not seen with the eyes,
yet what is recorded in the books,
and transmitted in the histories of the past,
when examined and discussed,
makes it certain that they exist.
It seems they specifically receive a unique *qì*,
endowed by nature,
and it is not something that can be achieved through accumulated learning.
As for guiding and nourishing one's life according to the correct principles,
to fulfill the span of one's life,
attaining over a thousand years at the highest level,
and several hundred years at the lowest,
this is indeed possible.
However, the people of the world are not meticulous,
and so none are able to achieve it.
Why do I say this?
Now, when taking medicine to induce sweating,
one might sometimes not succeed;
but once a feeling of shame gathers,
perspiration flows profusely.
If one has not eaten all morning,
one clamors for food;
yet Zēng Zǐ, harboring grief, was not hungry for seven days.
If one sits up late into the night,
one becomes drowsy and longs for sleep;
but if one harbors deep anxiety within,
one does not close one's eyes until dawn.
Stiff brushes to groom the sideburns,
and pure ale to brighten the face,
attain their effects only with effort;
but the anger of a brave man,
is a brilliant and extraordinary sight,
his hair standing upright and lifting his cap.
Speaking from this perspective,
the spirit's relation to the physical body,
is like a state having a ruler.
If the spirit is restless within,
the form will perish without;
just as when a ruler is deluded above,
the state falls into chaos below.
Now, for those farming during the era of Tāng,
if there is someone who manages a single instance of irrigation,
although in the end the crops will inevitably wither and rot,
the one that was irrigated will certainly be the last to dry up;
thus, the benefit of a single irrigation,
certainly cannot be denied.
Yet the world often says that a single fit of anger is not enough to encroach upon one's nature,
and a single moment of grief is not enough to harm the body;
they treat these lightly and indulge in them,
which is like not recognizing the benefit of a single irrigation,
yet expecting fine grain from parched seedlings.
Therefore, the superior person knows that the physical form relies on the spirit to stand,
and the spirit requires the form to exist.
Understanding that the principles of life are easily lost,
and knowing that a single error harms life.
Thus, they cultivate their nature to preserve the spirit,
and calm the mind to keep the body whole.
Love and hate do not dwell in their emotions,
and sorrow and joy do not linger in their thoughts.
Placid and without being affected,
their bodily *qì* is harmonious and balanced,
furthermore, they practice breathing exercises,
and ingest substances to nourish the body;
causing the form and spirit to be in harmony with each other,
so that both the internal and external are mutually aided.
Now, as for those who plant fields,
ten *hú* per *mǔ*,
is called a good field.
This is the common designation throughout the world.
They do not know that intensive plot-planting,
can yield over a hundred *hú*.
The field and the seed are the same,
but as for the differences in cultivation and nourishment,
the results and harvests are poles apart.
To say that a merchant cannot get ten times the price,
or that a farmer cannot hope for a hundred *hú*,
is to cling to the ordinary and fail to change.
Furthermore, beans make one heavy,
elm seeds make one sleepy,
the silk tree removes resentment,
and daylilies make one forget sorrow.
This is known by the foolish and the wise alike.
Pungent herbs harm the eyes,
and pufferfish is not nourishing,
this is recognized by the ordinary world.
Lice living on the head become black,
musk deer eat cypress and become fragrant,
necks in rugged terrain develop goiters,
and teeth in Jìn become yellow.
Extrapolating from this,
whatever *qì* is consumed permeates the nature and stains the body,
and all things respond accordingly.
Could it be that it only permeates to make one heavy,
and never to make one light?
That it only harms to make one dim,
and never to make one bright?
That it only fumes to make one yellow,
and never to make one strong?
That it only perfumes to make one fragrant,
and never to make one endure?
Therefore Shén Nóng said:
"Superior medicines nourish life,
middle medicines nourish nature";
this is because he truly knew the principles of nature and life,
and thus used supportive nourishment to attain mastery.
Yet the people of the world do not examine this,
seeing only the five grains,
and indulging only in sounds and colors;
their eyes are confused by dark and yellow colors,
their ears are occupied with licentious music;
rich flavors sear their internal organs,
sweet wine boils their intestines and stomach,
and fragrant scents rot their bone marrow.
Joy and anger confound their upright *qì*,
worries and thoughts wither their spirit,
and sorrow and pleasure bring disaster to their balanced purity.
With such a tiny body,
those that attack it are not just of one path;
with a body easily exhausted,
one receives enemies from both outside and within;
if the body is not wood or stone,
how can it last long?
For those who are extremely self-willed,
eating and drinking without moderation,
thereby giving rise to a hundred diseases.
Being tireless in the pursuit of lust,
leads to exhaustion and depletion.
Calamities from wind and cold,
and injuries from a hundred poisons.
Dying young midway because of many hardships,
the world all knows to mock or mourn them,
saying they were not good at maintaining life.
As for placing one's body in a way that loses the principle,
it is lost in the minute details,
accumulated minutiae become damage,
accumulated damage becomes decline,
from decline one gets white hair,
from white hair one gets old age,
from old age one gets the end,
all as if obscured and without a cause.
Those of mediocre intelligence and below,
call this nature.
Even if they have a bit of awakening and all sigh,
they regret only the beginning of what they encountered,
but do not know to be cautious of many dangers before they manifest.
This is like Huán Hóu harboring a fatal illness,
and being angry at Biǎn Què's foresight;
taking the day pain was felt,
as the beginning of the illness.
Harm is formed in the minute,
but it is only treated when it is prominent,
thus there are treatments that have no effect.
Galloping within the realm of ordinary people,
therefore one has a common lifespan.
Looking up and observing, looking down and examining,
there are none who are not like this.
They use the majority to prove themselves right,
using the similarity to comfort themselves,
saying the principles of heaven and earth,
are limited to this alone.
Even if they hear of the matters of nourishing life,
they judge it based on what they have seen,
saying it is not so.
Next, although their suspicion is slight,
they almost do not know from where to begin.
Next are those who exert themselves to take medicine,
for half a year or a year,
laboring without results;
their will becomes tired and fades,
and they abandon it halfway.
Or they add to it with a small ditch,
but drain it with the Wěilǘ abyss;
and yet they want to sit and wait for a clear reward.
Or they suppress emotions and restrain desires,
discarding honors and aspirations,
yet their cravings are always before their ears and eyes,
while what they hope for is dozens of years later.
Fearing to lose both,
they harbor hesitation within,
the heart battles within,
things entice from without,
the present and the distant conflict with each other,
and in this way, they fail again.
The ultimate thing is subtle and profound,
it can be known through principle,
but is difficult to recognize with the eyes.
For example, like the Yùzhāng tree,
it is only after seven years of growth that it can be recognized;
now, with a restless and competitive mind,
one treads the path of silent stillness;
the intention is fast but the matter is slow,
the hope is for the near but the response is far;
Therefore, none are able to bring it to completion.
For those who are indifferent do not seek it because they have seen no effects;
those who seek it lose their pursuit because they are not focused;
those who rely on only one aspect fail to achieve success because they are not comprehensive;
and those who chase after techniques drown themselves in minor arts.
In all cases such as these,
of those who desire it,
not one in ten thousand can succeed.
Those who are good at *yǎngshēng*,
however, are not like this.
Pure, empty, tranquil, and peaceful,
they have few private interests and scant desires.
Knowing that reputation and position damage virtue,
they disregard them and do not strive for them;
it is not that they desire them but forcibly restrain themselves.
Recognizing that rich flavors harm their nature,
they discard them and do not look back;
it is not that they are greedy but then suppress it.
External things that burden the heart are not retained;
spirit and *qì* alone shine forth in pure whiteness.
Vastly open and without worry or distress,
tranquilly still and without anxious thoughts,
they further maintain it with oneness
and nourish it with harmony.
As harmony and reason daily increase,
they become one with the *Dà Shùn*.
Then they are steamed with *língzhī*,
moistened with sweet springs,
warmed by the morning sun,
and soothed by the five strings.
In *wúwéi*, they find self-fulfillment;
their bodies are subtle and their hearts profound.
Forgetting joy, their happiness is sufficient;
leaving life behind, their bodies are preserved.
Proceeding in this manner,
they may perhaps compare in longevity to Xiàn Mén
and rival Wáng Qiáo in years.
How could it be that such things do not exist?
*Dá Nàn Yǎngshēng Lùn*, one piece.
The reply states:
The reason why wisdom is valued and action is esteemed
is because they can benefit life and enrich the self.
However, if one acts out of desire, then regret and humiliation arise;
if wisdom is exercised, then foresight is established.
When foresight is established, the will expands and things are accomplished;
when regret and humiliation arise, calamities accumulate and the self is endangered.
If these two are not harbored within but are engaged with the outside world,
they only suffice to bring disaster to the self,
and are not the means to enrich life.
Now, although desires and cravings stem from the person,
they are not the correctness of the *Dào* and *Dé*.
They are like wood having woodworms;
although produced by the wood,
they are not what is suitable for the wood.
Thus, when woodworms flourish, the wood rots;
when desires prevail, the self withers.
Consequently, desire and life do not stand together,
and fame and the self do not coexist;
this can be roughly understood.
Yet the world has not awakened to this,
taking the following of desires to be the attainment of life.
Although they have the sentiment of wanting to enrich life,
they do not recognize the principle of generating life.
Therefore, they move toward the ground of death.
For this reason, the people of antiquity
knew that wine and lust were sweet poison,
and discarded them as if they were abandoned things;
they recognized fame and rank as fragrant bait,
and walked away without looking back.
They ensured their actions were sufficient to support life,
without being excessive regarding material things,
knowing how to rectify their selves,
and not being preoccupied with external matters.
Turning their backs on what is harmful,
and turning toward what is beneficial,
this is the way to use wisdom to fulfill life.
Thus, the beauty of wisdom
is beautiful because it benefits life,
and not because it envies life for being precious.
It values its joy and harmony without entanglement;
how could one hate wisdom and slight the self,
or be diligent in desire and cheapen life?
Furthermore, that the Sages treasure the throne
and regard wealth and status as lofty
is because the ruler is noble as the *Tiānzǐ*,
and wealthy by possessing all within the four seas.
The people cannot exist without a sovereign,
and a sovereign cannot be established without honor.
Therefore, for the sake of the world, they honor the ruler’s position,
not for the sake of one individual do they value wealth and status.
It is also said:
"Wealth and status are what people desire,"
probably because in a declining age, people hate poverty and lowliness,
and love wealth and status.
Being unable to set aside glory and be at peace with poverty and lowliness,
the Sage constrains them to follow the Way.
If they cannot be prevented from competing, they should not be made to compete with all their strength;
therefore, he permits them to compete in spirit.
Since the *Zhōngyōng* cannot be attained,
he grants them the wild and the cautious.
This is merely worldly talk;
it does not say that the *Zhìrén* should be greedy for wealth and status.
The Sage governs the world only out of necessity,
taking the myriad things as his heart,
pardoning and being lenient with all living beings,
guiding himself by the Way,
and sharing in self-contentment with the world.
Solemnly taking non-action as his occupation,
and openly taking the world as a public trust.
Although occupying the ruler’s position
and receiving the homage of ten thousand states,
he is as composed as a common scholar receiving guests.
Although raising dragon banners
and wearing magnificent robes,
he is as indifferent as if wearing cloth garments.
Thus, ruler and minister forget each other above,
and the masses are self-sufficient in their homes below.
How could he encourage the common people to honor him,
carve up the world for his own selfishness,
regard wealth and status as lofty,
and desire them in his heart without end?
Furthermore, *Zǐwén* was appointed three times,
but his expression showed no added joy;
