*Liǔhuì* was dismissed three times,
but his countenance showed no added grief.
Why is this?
The honor of the *Lìngyǐn*
is not as noble as virtue and righteousness;
the lowliness of being thrice dismissed
does not harm the beauty of humble purity.
These two men attained wealth and status throughout their lives,
yet they did not let human rank entangle their hearts;
therefore, they viewed honor and disgrace as one.
Speaking from this perspective,
how could one say they had the sentiment of desiring wealth and status?
May I ask, if brocade clothes and embroidered robes
are not displayed in a dark room,
why must one consider the crowd
and constantly take praise and blame as joy and sorrow?
If it is so,
then those who desire something worry about obtaining it,
and having obtained it, they fear losing it;
once they worry about losing it, there is no length to which they will not go.
Being in a high position, how can they not be arrogant?
Holding a full vessel, how can it not overflow?
Seeking it, how can they not be improper?
Having obtained it, how can they not lose it?
Furthermore, when the *Jūnzǐ* speaks,
if it is good, then people from a thousand *lǐ* away will respond;
how could it depend on having many desires to value attainment?
Upholding the law and following principles,
not getting caught in the worldly net,
regarding being without fault as self-honor,
and regarding not serving in office as leisure.
Letting the mind wander in the Way and righteousness,
and resting in a humble room.
Serene and joyful without meeting obstacles,
and his spirit and vital energy are clear and unhindered.
Does he need glory and splendor
before he can be considered noble?
Tilling the soil for food,
raising silkworms for clothes,
with food and clothing sufficient for the person,
there is a surplus of the world’s wealth.
Like a thirsty person drinking from a river,
he is content and satisfied,
and does not envy the vast torrent.
Does he need to wait for accumulation and collection
before he can be considered wealthy?
The mind-set of the *Jūnzǐ* is like this.
He would take fame and rank as superfluous growths,
and material wealth as dust and dirt.
Of what use are wealth and status?
Thus, what is hard to obtain in the world
is not wealth,
nor is it glory;
the trouble is only that the mind is not satisfied!
For those whose minds are satisfied,
even if they plow the fields in pairs,
wear coarse cloth, and eat beans,
how could they not be self-contented?
For those who are not satisfied, even if they are nourished by the whole world
and entrusted with the myriad things,
they are still not pleased.
Thus, the satisfied do not need anything external,
while the unsatisfied need everything external.
Needing everything,
they are therefore never without lack wherever they go;
needing nothing,
they are therefore never without enough wherever they go.
Not letting glory and splendor indulge the will,
not letting obscurity and poverty follow the common customs.
Mingling and moving alongside the myriad things,
they cannot be affected by favor or disgrace;
this is to truly possess wealth and status.
Thus, regarding those who neglect nobility yet desire nobility,
lowliness reaches them;
thus, regarding those who forget wealth yet desire wealth,
poverty finds them.
This is the natural principle.
Nowadays, those who dwell in glory and splendor but worry,
even if they grow old with glory and splendor,
it only results in lifelong sorrow.
Therefore, *Lǎozǐ* said:
"No joy is greater than being without worry;
no wealth is greater than knowing contentment."
This is what is meant.
An objection says:
To feel and then think of the household,
to be hungry and then seek food,
is the natural principle.
Truly, these words are correct!
Now, I am not suggesting that one should not have a household or not eat,
but only that having a household and eating should attain their proper principle.
To desire without deliberation
is the movement of nature;
to feel only after conscious recognition
is the application of the intellect.
When nature moves,
it encounters objects and remains appropriate;
being satisfied, there is no excess.
When the intellect is applied,
it seeks based on feelings,
and continues without weariness.
Therefore, what the world suffers from,
and the source from which calamities arise,
always lies in the application of the intellect,
and not in the movement of nature.
Now, if a blind person encounters a household,
then Xī Shī and Mómǔ are the same to their feelings;
if one lacking the sense of taste forgets flavors,
then dregs and husks are as sweet as fine grains.
How could they recognize the worthy, the foolish, the beautiful, or the ugly,
so as to disturb the heart with love and hate?
The Jūnzǐ knows that the intellect and wisdom harm life through lack of constancy,
and desires harm nature through the pursuit of objects.
Therefore, when the intellect is used, he restrains it with tranquility;
when nature moves, he regulates it with harmony,
making the intellect stop at tranquility,
and nature find sufficiency in harmony.
Thereafter, the spirit becomes pure through silence,
and the body is completed through harmony,
removing burdens and eliminating harm,
to be reborn with the other.
This is what is called not seeing what is desirable,
so that the heart is not disturbed.
Even if flavors often stain the mouth,
and sounds and colors have already opened the heart,
they can be dispelled with ultimate reason,
and overcome with careful calculation.
Why do I say this?
One who desires office does not consider the ruler's position;
one who thinks of the household does not contemplate his relatives.
Why is this?
Knowing what cannot be obtained,
then the thought does not arise in the heart.
Thus, the lover of wine restrains himself before poisoned liquor;
the greedy eater endures hunger before tainted meat.
Knowing the principles of good and bad fortune,
one turns away from them without confusion,
and abandons them without doubt.
How could one regret not having been able to drink to intoxication or eat greedily earlier?
Furthermore, regarding the concubines of the inn,
the ugly one was valued because she considered herself ugly;
the beautiful one was held cheap because she considered herself beautiful.
The forms of beauty and ugliness were in the eyes,
yet honor and lowliness were different;
the sentiment of right and wrong was established first,
so beauty and ugliness could not shift it.
If it is said that reason is sufficient within,
and one rides upon the One to govern the external,
what object could be a burden?
From this perspective,
if the nature and Qi are naturally in harmony,
then there is no distress from restrictions;
if the emotions and will are naturally calm,
then there is no pent-up frustration without passage.
The many burdens of the world
are merely due to a lack of clarity in vision.
Furthermore, it is the nature of ordinary people:
what is far away,
though great, is always neglected;
what is near,
though small, is always attended to.
What is the reason for this?
It is truly because the immediate and the distant displace each other,
and knowledge and vision have different sentiments.
Refraining from inner chambers during the three-year mourning period
is a prohibition of the rites,
and no one violates it;
yet wine and lust are the enemies of the body,
and no one can abandon them.
From this perspective,
even if a ritual prohibition is immediate, though small, it is not violated;
while the body's enemy is distant, though great, it is not abandoned.
Yet if one were to hold the maps of the world in his left hand,
while with his right hand he immediately harmed his body,
even a fool would not do it.
It is clear that the world is lighter than one's body,
and wine and lust are lighter than the world;
this too can be known.
Yet people of the world sacrifice themselves for them,
dying without regret;
this is using what is heavy to seek what is light.
Is this not turning away from the distant to pursue the immediate?
The wise person is not like this.
He examines the weight of things and then moves;
he weighs gain and loss to position his person;
the principles of the immediate and the distant are the same to him;
therefore, he guards against the distant as if it were near,
and is as cautious of the subtle as of the manifest;
walking alone through the gate of all wonders,
thus from beginning to end he has no worries.
Between this and those who indulge in desires to satisfy their whims,
what a vast difference there is!
Objection:
Sages exhaust principles and fully realize their nature,
so they should enjoy longevity;
yet Yáo and Kǒng at most reached a hundred years,
and the lesser ones only seventy.
Could it be that they were negligent in the practices of nourishing life?
According to the discussion, although Yáo and Kǒng received a limited lifespan by fate,
they practiced nourishing life to complete their natural years.
This is the result of exhausting principles;
it is not that they did not nourish life to reach a hundred years.
Furthermore, Zhòngní exhausted principles and fully realized his nature,
yet only reached seventy;
while a peasant, though worn out and ignorant,
may reach a hundred and twenty.
If we took the ultimate subtlety of Zhòngní
and supported it with the ultimate simplicity of the peasant,
then the theory of a thousand years of life—
what would be strange about it?
Moreover, as for the Sages,
some diminished themselves for the sake of the world,
manifesting conduct and displaying merit,
causing the world to admire them,
as in moving three times and completing a capital;
some ate meagerly and worked hard,
managing the four quarters,
their hearts labored and their bodies exhausted,
their pace losing its rhythm;
some devised secret strategies,
extending even to weapons of war,
with majesty, power, and slaughter,
struggling for merit and profit.
Some cultivated themselves to highlight impurity,
displayed wisdom to startle the foolish,
relying on a high reputation in their generation,
and becoming a standard for the world;
also being diligent in teaching and skillful in leading,
gathering three thousand disciples,
their mouths weary from discussion,
their bodies exhausted from bowing,
their appearance like one saving a child,
their gaze as if managing the four seas.
Their spirits raced toward the ends of profit and harm,
their hearts galloped along the paths of honor and disgrace;
in the blink of an eye,
they have already twice traversed beyond the universe.
If one compares this to looking inward and listening backward,
cherishing Qi and husbanding the essence;
being bright and reaching in all four directions,
while being without attachment or action;
leaving the world and sitting in oblivion,
to treasure nature and preserve the truth;
I cannot see them as the same.
Now, I am not saying that the pine and cypress
are no different from the elm and willow.
However, the life of the pine and cypress
each follows its nature through good cultivation.
If one grows a pine in ashy soil,
it will wither and fall in mid-life.
If planted on a steep cliff,
it flourishes more daily.
This is one perspective on nourishing the physical form.
Dòugōng had no special diet or regimen,
yet he reached a hundred and eighty years.
Was it not because playing the qín harmonized his heart?
This is one proof of nourishing the spirit.
Summer silkworms live eighteen days,
while winter silkworms live over thirty days;
though they cannot exceed their seasonal lifespan,
the care they receive can be more than doubled.
Those kept warm and fat die early;
those kept cool and lean are exhausted later;
this can certainly be recognized.
Stable horses are cared for but not ridden,
and they all live for sixty years.
Those whose bodies are exhausted wither quickly;
those whose forms are kept whole are hard to kill;
this too can be known.
The wealthy and noble often die young,
for many are those who cut them down;
the rustic people often live long,
for few are those who harm them.
This too can be seen.
Now, if one can make the eyes function like the blind,
and the mouth have the same taste as one lacking the sense,
keeping away the tools that harm life,
and managing the things that benefit nature,
then one can begin to speak of nourishing nature and life.
The objection says:
Shénnóng initiated the beginning of eating grain;
birds and beasts use it to fly and run,
and the common people use it to see and breathe.
Now, I do not say that the five grains were not initiated by Shénnóng;
but having spoken of superior medicines,
why also initiate the five grains?
It is because superior medicines are rare and scarce,
arduous and difficult to obtain,
while the five grains are easy to cultivate,
and farming can be sustained for a long time.
This is how to save the hundred surnames and prevent premature death;
they are preserved together.
Only the worthy set their will on the great;
the unworthy merely set theirs on the small.
These both come from the same person.
As for Dāngguī stopping pain,
its use is never-ending;
as for plowing and clearing land with plow and share,
one follows this without ceasing.
Why, when it comes to nourishing life,
do you disregard and not discuss it?
This is likely being obsessed with what was first practiced
and finding strange what is yet unknown.
Furthermore, the plains have things like dates and chestnuts,
and the ponds have things like water caltrops and fox nuts;
although they are not superior medicines,
they are still [superior] to the devotion given to millet and grain.
How can one say the tools for seeing and breathing
consist only of the five grains?
It is also said:
"The fragrance of millet and grain
truly brings down the spirits."
Duckweed and pondweed
are no match for rich delicacies;
puddle water and runoff
are no match for heavy fermented wine.
Offered in the ancestral temple,
they move the spirits to descend with blessings.
Thus we know the spirits feast on virtue and sincerity
and do not take what nourishes them as the source of life.
It is like the nine regions reporting on their duties,
each contributing local products
to demonstrate their sincerity.
It is also said:
When meat and grain enter the body,
the benefit does not exceed ten days,
to clarify the proof of what is suitable for life.
This is how the body is burdened.
Now, I do not say that meat and grain provide no benefit in filling the body;
I only mean that extending life is not a match for superior medicines.
Please allow me to use this as a counter-argument.
Knowing that wheat is better than beans
and rice is superior to millet
comes from recognizing them through their effects.
Suppose there were a region without rice and millet;
they would surely value beans and wheat as precious nourishment,
saying nothing could be superior.
Thus the people of the world do not know that superior medicines are better than rice and millet,
just as they maintain that beans and wheat are superior to mugwort and weeds,
yet they insist that the world lacks rice and millet.
If one could rely on medicine to sustain oneself forever,
then the insignificance of rice and millet
would clearly be known.
The gentleman knows it is like this;
therefore, he conforms to what is suitable for the principle of nature
and relies on wondrous substances to nourish the body.
He plants the "mystic root" at the Chūjiǔ
and inhales the morning glow to sustain the spirit.
Now, if one uses spring wine for longevity,
then I have not heard of the Gāoyáng region having any yellow-haired elders;
if one considers being well-fed and joyful as worthiness,
then I have not heard of a guest at a grand feast reaching a hundred years.
Moreover, Rǎn Shēng suffered from illness,
and Yán Zǐ died young.
In bountiful years, there is much illness;
in famine years, there is little disease.
Thus, the Dì eat rice and develop leprosy
and sores;
if they get grain, their blood floats;
if horses feed on millet, their legs become heavy;
if wild geese eat grain, their bodies become stagnant.
Speaking from this,
birds and beasts need not repay their merit to the five grains,
and the common people need not receive virtue from the fields.
Yet people exhaust their strength to cultivate them
and sacrifice their lives to struggle for them;
for nourishing parents or offering to the venerable,
there are only chrysanthemums, water oats, fine grains, and rice;
for betrothals, offerings, and grand gatherings,
there are only meat dishes and fine wine.
But they do not know that these are all muddy, sticky, and greasy,
easily turning to mush and quickly rotting.
Though sweet and fragrant at first,
once they enter the body's foul places,
they exhaust and disgrace the spirit
and pollute the six fǔ organs.
Stagnant and filthy vapors steam up,
naturally giving rise to disasters and pests.
This is the ladder to gluttony and excess,
where a hundred diseases attach themselves.
Those who taste them lose their sense of flavor;
those who consume them have a short lifespan.
How can they compare to flowing springs and sweet nectar,
or jasper stamens and jade blossoms?
Golden elixir and stone mushrooms,
purple Zhī and Huángjīng.
These all contain the essence of various spirits
and uniquely produce wondrous life.
Their pure fragrance is hard to dissipate;
their harmonious Qi is full and overflowing.
They wash the five organs like snow,
clearing and brightening them.
Those who sip them find their bodies light.
Furthermore, they refine the skeleton and transform the Qi,
dye the bones and soften the sinews.
They wash away grime and moisten filth,
and the will rises to the blue clouds.
If it goes like this,
what need is there for the nourishment of the five grains?
Moreover, the mason wasp has young,
and the mud dauber carries them away—
this is a transformation of nature.
Oranges crossing the river become zhǐ—
changing soil and transforming,
this is a difference of form.
Absorbing the Qi of what is eaten,
returning the essence and changing the nature—
how could that not be possible?
Thus Chìfǔ refined cinnabar to turn his hair red;
Juānzǐ used the essence of Zhú to prolong his life;
Wòquán used pine seeds to make his eyes square;
Chìsōng used crystal to ride the smoke;
Wùguāng used cattails and leeks to grow long ears;
Qióngshū used stone marrow to halt the years;
Fānghuí used mica to undergo transformation;
Chāngróng used pénglúi to change her face.
Examples of this kind
cannot be recorded in detail.
Who says the five grains are the best
and that superior medicines are of no benefit?
Furthermore, you criticize that for a thousand years,
the eye has not seen such things
and say there is no such person.
Then I ask the speaker:
if you saw a person of a thousand years,
how would you distinguish him?
If you wish to compare him by form,
then he is no different from other people;
if you wish to verify him by years,
then the morning mushroom has no way to know the end and beginning of a month,
and the mayfly has no way to recognize the divine tortoise.
Thus, even if a person of a thousand years were in the markets or the court,
they certainly could not be identified by someone with a short lifespan.
Péngzǔ lived seven hundred years,
Ānqī lived a thousand years—
yet those with narrow views say the books are false records.
Liú Gēn slept far away and did not eat;
some say he just happened to be able to endure hunger.
Zhòngdū was naked in winter yet his body was warm,
and wore furs in summer yet his body was cool;
Huán Tán said he just happened to endure cold and heat.
Lǐ Shǎojūn recognized the jade bowl of Huán Gōng,
yet Ruǎn Shēng called it a lucky guess.
And it is known that Yáo abdicated the empire to Xǔ Yóu,
yet Yáng Xióng said it was done out of a love for the grand.
In all cases such as these,
those above use Zhōu and Kǒng as their gatekeepers,
dedicating their will to a single sincerity;
those below use desires as their whip and spur,
wanting to stop but being unable to.
They gallop within the teachings of the world
and struggle for cleverness between honor and disgrace,
diminishing themselves by following the majority
and not letting their thoughts stray from their station,
causing extraordinary events to be excluded from what is seen
and wondrous principles to be cut off from common discourse.
As for speaking of penetrating transformations and reaching the subtle,
they have never heard of it.
Long resentful of living in leisure,
they call it having no joy;
deeply regretting the lack of meat dishes,
they call it self-inflicted sorrow.
Taking wine and beauty as their sustenance,
they call long life boring.
Thus, that which you consider joy
must involve four-horse carriages and strings of riders
and eating from a table ten feet square before you.
To wait for such things before being satisfied
and to call this the natural principle of Heaven
is all to enslave the body to things
and to lose the will to desire.
Investigating the reality of nature and life,
this has encumbered what you have discussed.
A thirsty person sees only water;
a drinker seeks only wine;
everyone knows this arises from an ailment.
Now, if one takes following desires as attaining one's nature,
then the thirsty and the drinkers would not be ill.
That those who indulge in excess are not at fault,
and that those like Jié and Zhí were both following their nature,
is not the intention of this treatise to clarify the ultimate principle.
Indeed, the ultimate principle is truly subtle
and easily submerged in the world,
yet perhaps it can be sought within oneself and then realized,
rather than comparing external things to know it.
From youth to old age,
a person's likes and dislikes decrease and change,
having periods of flourishing and decline;
what was enjoyed in childhood
is discarded in adulthood;
what was initially disdained
is eventually valued.
When experiencing what one likes,
one says it cannot be taken away;
when encountering what one loathes,
one says it cannot bring joy;
yet when positions are reversed,
the feelings change from the beginning.
If appetites and desires can change,
how can one know that what is currently relished
will not become like rotting flesh?
Or that what was previously despised
will not become rare and beautiful?
Suppose a lowly servant suddenly rises to become a high official (Qīng Yǐn),
then those like gatekeepers
he will slight and leave behind.
Speaking from this perspective,
all these are merely the narrow feelings of a single realm;
how could they be unchanging?
Furthermore, for a hungry diner,
when about to obtain what they desire,
their joyful feelings and mind are focused on it;
after being full and satisfied,
they are relieved and distance themselves from it,
or even feel disgust.
Thus, there are times when glory, wine, and beauty can be distanced.
Pythons (Ránshé) are prized in the land of Yuè,
but those in Zhōngguó loathe them upon encounter;
ceremonial robes (Fǔfú) are valued in Huáxià,
but the land of the naked (Luǒguó) would discard them upon receiving them.
When they are useless,
they are all like the pythons of Zhōngguó
and the ceremonial robes of the Luǒguó.
Taking Great Harmony (Dàhé) as the ultimate joy,
then glory is not worth a look;
taking Tranquility (Tiándàn) as the ultimate flavor,
then wine and beauty are not worth admiring.
If there is a place for the mind to be satisfied,
the pleasures of the vulgar world
are all but dung and soil;
how could they be worth longing for?
Today’s debaters do not see the essence of ultimate joy
and are content to shorten their years and damage their lives
to pursue their desires.
This is Lǐ Sī turning his back on Confucianism
to sacrifice himself for the desires of a single morning;
or Zhǔfù giving vent to his indignation,
thinking only of the flavors of the five tripods.
Furthermore, those in the dried-fish market (Bàosì) enjoy themselves
while devaluing orchids (Lánchǎi),
just as a sea bird faces the great sacrificial feast (Tàiláo) and grieves long,
or Marquis Wén (Wén Hóu) hears elegant music (Yǎyuè) and stops his ears.
Therefore, taking glory as the equipment for life,
one says that even saving ten thousand generations is not enough for joy.
All these involve having no master within
and borrowing external things for joy;
though external things may be abundant,
sorrow is also fully present.
If one has a master within,
using inner joy to influence the external;
though there are no bells or drums,
joy is already complete.
Thus, the one who attains their will
is not one with high carriages and crowns (Xuánmiǎn);
the one who has ultimate joy
is not one with abundant possessions.
Gain and loss cannot burden them.
Furthermore, if parents are ill
and recover after distress,
then worry and joy are used together.
From this perspective,
it can be known that it is better to have no joy.
Thus, is no-joy not the ultimate joy?
Therefore, following the harmony of Heaven to be natural (Zìrán),
taking the Way and Virtue (Dàodé) as teachers and friends,
enjoying the changes of Yīn and Yáng,
and attaining the permanence of long life (Chángshēng);
entrusting one's body to nature (Zìrán),
and being as immortal as Heaven and Earth—
who could enjoy this?
There are five difficulties in nourishing life (Yǎngshēng):
fame and profit not being extinguished,
this is the first difficulty.
Joy and anger not being removed,
this is the second difficulty.
Sound and beauty not being cast away,
this is the third difficulty.
Flavors not being cut off,
this is the fourth difficulty.
Spiritual thoughts being constantly stirred,
this is the fifth difficulty.
If these five exist,
though the heart hopes for slowing aging,
the mouth recites ultimate words,
one chews the flowery essence,
and breathes the essence of the sun,
one cannot help but waver in one's conduct
and have one's lifespan cut short.
If these five are absent from the breast,
then faith and obedience will daily increase,
and Profound Virtue (Xuándé) will daily become complete.
Without praying for joy, there will be blessings;
without seeking longevity, it will extend of itself.
This is the effect of the great principle of nourishing life (Yǎngshēng).
However, there are some whose conduct surpasses that of Zēng and Mǐn,
who follow benevolence and righteousness,
whose actions stem from centered harmony,
and who have no great burdens,
they then say that human principles are complete
and take pride in this.
But without dispelling joy and anger
and calming the spirit and energy,
yet desiring to repel old age and extend years—
I have never heard of such a thing.
Some maintain their will and aspire to the ancients,
not seeking glory in name or position,
and thus place themselves above those who rush about.
Some use wisdom to manage the world
and not encounter disaster,
thus valuing themselves for this.
This is only equivalent to using one's body to match the age of elders in one's local community.
As for preserving life,
it is entirely lacking.
Some abandon the world and do not join the crowd,
their will and spirit being harmonious and pure,
yet without cutting off grains and eating numinous mushrooms,
it is of no benefit for a short lifespan.
Or if fine grains (Qiónghóu) are already stored,
and the six types of energy are simultaneously mastered,
and one can contain light and look inward,
concentrate the spirit and return to the uncarved block (Pǔ),
lodging the heart on the shore of the dark mystery (Xuánmíng),
and containing energy at the shore of the Great Void—
then there is old age that can be repelled
and years that can be extended.
All these several factors must be combined for use
and cannot be without each other.
Like the shafts, axles, wheels, and linchpins,
not one can be missing from a chariot.
Yet if people have a partial view,
each will suffer from what they provide;
Dān Bào managed the internal but forgot the external,
Zhāng Yì hurried toward the external and lost the internal.
Qí suffered defeat because of its caution at Jìxī,
Qín exhausted itself by preparing for the Róng and Dí,
these are all disasters of not balancing both.
Accumulating good and practicing faith,
the world has often heard of this;
being careful in speech
and moderate in food and drink,
scholars recognize this.
Beyond this,
none perhaps know.
I request that those who have awakened first
speak to those who will awaken in the future.
Treatise on Sound Having No Sorrow or Joy (Shēng Wú Āi Lè Lùn).
A guest from Qín asked the Host of Dōngyě:
"I have heard it said in previous discourses:
'The music of a well-governed age is peaceful and joyful;
the music of a perishing state is sorrowful and longing.'
Order and chaos reside in the government,
and musical sounds respond to them.
Therefore, feelings of sorrow and longing
are expressed through metal and stone,
while manifestations of peace and joy
are formed in pipes and strings.
Furthermore, when Zhòngní heard the Sháo music,
he recognized the virtue of Yú Shùn;
when Jì Zhá listened to the strings,
he knew the customs of the various states.
These are established matters of the past
which the former worthies did not doubt.
Now you alone believe that sound has neither sorrow nor joy;
what is the reasoning for this?
If you have a fine instruction,
I now request to hear your explanation."
The Host replied:
"This concept has long been stagnant,
and no one has been willing to rescue it.
Consequently, throughout the ages,
names and realities have been confused.
Now, receiving your guidance,
I shall speak of one aspect of it.
When Heaven and Earth join their virtues,
the myriad things value life.
Cold and heat alternate,
and the Five Elements are thus completed.
Therefore, they are manifested as the five colors
and expressed as the five notes.
The production of musical sounds
is like the existence of odors and flavors between Heaven and Earth.
Their goodness or badness,
even if encountering turbid chaos,
remains as it is in essence,
without changing.
How could they alter their character because of love or hate,
or change their measure because of sorrow or joy?
When Gōng and Shāng are gathered and arranged,
and the sounds achieve harmony,
this is the ultimate wish of the human heart
and the focus of passions and desires.
The ancients knew that passions must not be indulged
and desires must not be pushed to the extreme;
therefore, according to their application,
they always established constraints for them,
so that sorrow would not lead to injury
and joy would not lead to excess.
Following events and names,
things were given their titles.
Wailing is called sorrow;
singing is called joy.
This is the general distinction.
Yet when one speaks of 'joy, joy,'
is it merely about bells and drums?
When one speaks of 'sorrow, sorrow,'
is it merely about wailing and weeping?
Speaking from this perspective,
jade and silk are not the reality of ritual respect,
and song and dance are not the essence of sorrow.
How can this be clarified?
In distant lands with different customs,
singing and wailing differ;
if one were to use them interchangeably,
some might feel joy upon hearing wailing,
and some might feel grief upon hearing singing.
Yet the underlying emotions of sorrow and joy are the same.
Now, if using identical emotions
gives rise to ten thousand different sounds,
does this not prove that musical sounds have no fixed nature?
However, when sounds are harmonious and well-proportioned,
they move people most deeply.
The weary sing of their labors;
the successful dance to their achievements.
When there is a heart of grief within,
it results in intense and sorrowful words.
When words are arranged, they become poetry;
when sounds are arranged, they become music.
Chanted together in a mixture,
and listened to in a gathering,
the heart is moved by the harmonious sounds,
and the emotions are stirred by the bitter words.
Before the sighs have ended,
tears and weeping flow forth.
A sorrowful heart is stored within
and only breaks forth upon encountering harmonious sounds.
Harmonious sounds have no image,
while the sorrowful heart has a master.
When a sorrowful heart with a master
relies on imageless harmonious sounds,
that which it perceives
is nothing but sorrow.
How could it then understand that the 'blowing of the myriad things' is different
yet each is allowed to cease of itself?
The flow of customs
eventually constitutes governance.
Therefore, the state historians clarify the gains and losses of political education,
examine the prosperity and decline of the state airs,
and chant of human nature and character
to admonish those above.
Thus it is said:
'The music of a perishing state is sorrowful and longing.'
Joy, anger, sorrow, delight,
love, hate, shame, and fear—
all these eight
are the means by which the people interact with things and convey emotions;
they belong to distinct categories
and must not overflow their bounds.
Flavors are designated as sweet or bitter.
Now, if Jiǎ is worthy and my heart loves him,
and Yǐ is foolish and my feelings hate him,
then the love and hate should belong to me,
while the worthiness and foolishness should belong to them.
Can we, because of my love, call him the 'loved person,'
or because of my hate, call him the 'hated person'?
Can what is liked be called a 'joyful flavor,'
or what is resented be called an 'angry flavor'?
From this perspective,
the external and internal have different functions,
and 'the other' and 'the self' have different names.
Musical sounds should naturally take goodness or badness as their essence,
which has nothing to do with sorrow or joy.
Sorrow and joy should naturally break forth after the heart is moved,
which has no connection to musical sounds.
When both name and reality are discarded,
then the truth can be clearly seen.
Furthermore, when Jìzǐ was in Lǔ,
he collected poems and observed rituals
to distinguish the Fēng and the Yǎ.
How could he have relied solely on sound to determine good or bad?
Also, when Zhòngní heard the Sháo,
he marveled at its consistency;
this was why he sighed in admiration.
Why must it be that he recognized the virtue of Yú Shùn through the sound
before he could praise it?
Now that I have roughly clarified this one aspect,
you may consider yourself to have grasped more than half of it."
The guest from Qín challenged, saying:
"In the eight directions there are different customs,
and singing and wailing differ in ten thousand ways;
yet the emotions of sorrow and joy
cannot help but be revealed.
For the heart moves within,
and sound issues from the heart.
Though it may be entrusted to other tones
or rely on remaining sounds,
those who are skilled in listening and observing
will naturally perceive it and not let it pass by.
In the past, when Bó Yá played the qín,
Zhōng Zǐ knew his intent;
when the slave struck the stone chimes,
Zǐ Chǎn recognized the sorrow in his heart;
when a man of Lǔ wailed in the morning,
Yán Yuān discerned it was a parting of the living.
As for these several gentlemen,
did they really depend on wisdom from ordinary tones
or borrow proof from melodies and measures?
When the heart is distressed, the form moves accordingly;
when the emotions are sad, the sound becomes sorrowful.
This is a natural resonance
that cannot be escaped.
Only those with divine illumination can master its essence.
Those who are capable do not find many sounds difficult;
those who are incapable do not find few sounds easy.
Now, one cannot, because of not having met a skilled listener,
say that sound has no principle that can be observed;
or seeing the many variations of local customs,
say that sounds have no sorrow or joy.
You also say:
The worthy should not be spoken of with love,
and the foolish should not be spoken of with hate.
However, it is because there are the worthy that love arises,
and because there are the foolish that hate is formed;
it is just that their names should not be shared.
The arising of sorrow and joy
also has a cause from which it follows.
This means that the voice makes me sorrowful,
and the music makes me joyful.
If sorrow and joy come from sound,
then it becomes a reality;
how can name and reality both be gone?
You also say:
Jì Zǐ selected poems and observed rites
to distinguish between the Fēng and the Yǎ;
Zhòng Ní sighed at the consistency of the Sháo music,
and thus he lamented.
What kind of words are these?
Furthermore, when Shī Xiāng played the melody,
Zhòng Ní saw the appearance of Wén Wáng;
when Shī Juān presented the tune,
Zǐ Yě recognized the music of a fallen state.
Did they really have to lecture on the poems before speaking,
or study the rites before making an evaluation?
These were all instances of divine subtlety and unique insight,
not requiring a long stay or many days of listening
before summarizing the fortune or misfortune;
thus, previous histories regard them as beautiful anecdotes.
Now you, with your trifling and limited knowledge,
take what you see as the limit,
is this not slandering the past sages' insight into the subtle,
and betraying the Master's wondrous observation?"
The host replied:
"The challenge says:
Although singing and wailing vary in ten thousand ways,
those skilled in listening and observing will naturally perceive it,
not needing wisdom from ordinary tones,
nor borrowing proof from melodies and measures;
Zhōng Zǐ and his kind are examples of this.
This implies that one whose heart is sad,
though talking, laughing, drumming, or dancing,
or one whose feelings are cheerful,
though beating the breast and sighing,
still cannot control the external form to hide themselves,
or deceive an observer with ambiguities.
It assumes that even if sound is inconstant,
one still claims it must have sorrow or joy.
You also say:
Jì Zǐ listened to the sounds
to know the customs of the various states;
Shī Xiāng played the melody,
and Zhòng Ní saw the appearance of Wén Wáng.
According to what you say,
this means the merit and virtue of Wén Wáng,
and the prosperity or decline of customs,
can all be represented in sounds.
The weight of the sounds
can be transmitted to later generations,
and the skill of Xiāng and Juān
can be grasped in the future.
If this were so,
then the Sān Huáng and Wǔ Dì
would not be cut off from today;
why should it only be these few instances?
If this were truly the case,
then the melody of Wén Wáng would have a fixed measure,
and the music of Sháo and Wǔ would have a set number,
which could not be mixed with other variations
or played with remaining sounds.
Then what was previously called the inconstancy of sound
and Zhōng Zǐ's connection by category
would stumble here.
If the inconstancy of sound
and Zhōng Zǐ's connection by category
are indeed true,
then Zhòng Ní's insight into the subtle
and Jì Zhá's skill in listening
are surely also false;
these are all reckless records by common scholars,
wishing to make the events divine and inventing them after the fact.
They wish to make the world confused about the Way of sound
and not speak of the principles of nature;
pushing everything to this extreme,
they make the divine and subtle difficult to know,
lamenting that they did not encounter a wondrous listener in their time,
admiring the ancients and sighing for themselves;
this is how they greatly deceive later generations.
Now, in deducing by category and distinguishing things,
one should first seek them in the principles of nature.
Once the principle is settled,
then one borrows ancient meanings to clarify it.
Now, without having grasped it in the heart,
you rely heavily on former words as evidence for your talk;
from now on,
I fear even a clever calculator could not record them all.
You also challenge by saying:
The arising of sorrow and joy
is like love and hate following from the worthy and the foolish;
this means voice makes me sorrowful
and music makes me joyful.
If sorrow and joy come from sound,
then it becomes a reality.
Now, the five colors have beauty and ugliness,
and the five sounds have goodness and badness;
this is the nature of things.
As for loving and not loving,
liking and not liking,
these are changes in human emotions.
The principle that governs things
stops only here.
However, none of these are prepared within
but await things to be completed.
As for sorrow and joy, they come about through events,
first met in the heart,
but relying on harmonious sound
to manifest themselves.
Thus, the previous discourse already clarified its inconstancy,
and now I use this talk again to correct the names and titles.
I do not say that sorrow and joy originate from sounds,
like love and hate arise from the worthy and the foolish.
Yet, the way harmonious sound moves the human heart
is like how wine brings out the human nature.
Wine is characterized by sweetness and bitterness,
while the drunkard uses joy and anger.
Seeing happiness and distress as being triggered by sound
and saying that sound has sorrow and joy,
is like seeing joy and anger as being driven by wine
and saying that wine has the principle of joy and anger."
The guest from Qín challenged, saying:
"Observing the breath and picking up the colors
is common practice throughout the world.
When the heart changes within,
the color responds on the outside;
it is clearly visible,
so you, sir, do not doubt it.
Now, sound
is the stirring of the breath;
the heart moves in response to feelings,
and sound is issued according to the changes.
When the heart has strength or decline,
the sound also rises or falls.
Both are employed by the same body,
so why should you doubt sound alone?
If joy and anger are manifest in the complexion,
sorrow and joy should also be formed in sounds.
Sound naturally should have sorrow and joy,
but the ignorant cannot recognize it;
as for Zhōng Zǐ and his kind,
even if they encounter inconstant sounds,
they see them clearly and uniquely.
Now, a blind person faces a wall and is unaware,
while Lí Lóu can see an autumn hair at a distance of a hundred spans;
speaking from this,
clarity and darkness have different capabilities.
One cannot keep to a small measure
and doubt the observation of Lí Lóu;
or hold to mediocre hearing
and suspect the acuity of Zhōng Zǐ.
These all say that the ancients made reckless records."
The Host replied:
"The objection states:
The heart responds to stimuli and moves,
and sound is emitted following these changes.
If the heart is vigorous or declining,
the sound likewise rises or falls.
The emotions of sorrow and joy
must manifest in voices and sounds.
Those like Zhōng Zǐ,
even when encountering sounds that are not constant,
see through them with singular clarity.
If it must be as you say,
then the satiety of a coarse person,
the hunger at Shǒuyáng,
the grievance of Biàn Hé,
the sorrow of Bó Qí,
the suppressed anger of Xiàngrú,
and the terror of Bù Zhān,
truly represent a thousand changes and a hundred states.
If each were made to sing a song,
or to pluck a few notes on the strings,
then those like Zhōng Zǐ
would each discern their true feelings.
As a listener of sound,
do you not change your thoughts based on whether the sounds are few or many?
As an observer of feelings,
do you not distinguish between the large and the small?
If they emerge from the same body,
one expects to recognize them.
Suppose they come from an external source,
then those like Zǐ Yě
should also again handle the pitch-pipes and blow the tubes
to examine their tones,
to know the vigor or decline of the Nánfēng,
and to distinguish between the licentious and the upright in the Yǎ and Zhèng styles.
Eating pungent food and laughing heartily,
or smoke in the eyes and weeping in grief,
both result in the discharge of tears.
If Dí Yá were to taste them,
he certainly would not say that joyful tears are sweet
while sorrowful tears are bitter;
this can be known.
Why is this?
Muscle fluids and bodily sweat
are forced out by pressure
and are not governed by sorrow or joy.
It is like filtering wine with a bag;
although the tools for pressing differ,
the flavor of the wine does not change.
Since sounds all emerge from the same body,
why should they alone contain the principles of sorrow and joy?
Furthermore, the Xiánchí, Liùjīng,
Dàzhāng, and Sháoxià
are the supreme musics of the former kings,
used to move heaven and earth and affect ghosts and gods.
Now, if one must say that sound invariably reflects the physical form and transmits the heart,
then for this to be supreme music,
it could not be entrusted to blind musicians or chroniclers;
a Sage would have to manage the strings and pipes himself
for the elegant tones to be fully realized.
Shùn ordered Kuí to strike the stones and pat the stones;
the eight tones were made harmonious,
and gods and men were in harmony.
Speaking from this,
although supreme music awaits a Sage for its creation,
it is not necessary for the Sage to perform it personally.
Why?
Sounds have a natural harmony
that is not tied to human emotions.
Harmonious tones
are completed in metal and stone;
the sound of supreme harmony
is obtained from pipes and strings.
Even a tiny hair has a form that can be observed,
thus the keen-sighted and the blind differ in their ability to distinguish light and dark.
If you try to temper water with water,
what difference could there be?"
The guest from Qín objected:
"Although many of your analogies are obscure
and invite challenge,
yet the grand principles
must lead to a conclusion.
Like Gélú hearing the lowing of a cow
and knowing that its three calves were destined for sacrifice;
Shī Kuàng blowing the pitch-pipes
and knowing the Nánfēng was weak
and the Chǔ army would surely be defeated;
the mother of Yángshé hearing a child cry
and discerning the ruin of the family.
All these matters
were proven in former ages,
and therefore all were recorded.
Inferring from this,
then vigor and decline, good and bad fortune,
are all present in sound.
If you now say again that this is all false and deceptive,
then the words of the past and the ancient records
would all be discarded objects,
of no use.
In terms of general discourse,
this is not something one can be at ease with.
If you can clarify the reasons for this
and reveal their origins,
so that both theories may be reconciled,
I would like to hear it again."
The Host replied:
“I thought that for one capable of inferring three corners from one,
who grasps the meaning and forgets the words,
the previous argument was brief and not detailed.
Now that you trouble me again with circular objections,
how could I dare not exhaust my efforts for you?
As for the Lǔ cow being able to know that the sacrificial calendar meant its death,
mourning that its three calves would not survive,
harboring sorrow for a whole year,
and complaining to Gě Lú—
this would mean its mind is the same as a human’s,
differing only in its beastly form;
this is also what I doubt.
Moreover, cows are not of the human race,
and there is no way for communication between them.
If one says birds and beasts all possess this capacity,
and that Gě Lú received a nature
such that he alone understood it;
this would be matching their speech and discussing their affairs,
just like a translator passing on foreign words.
It would not be a case of examining the sounds to know their emotions,
and thus it is not a proper basis for a challenge.
If one says that a knowledgeable person
should be able to understand whatever they encounter,
knowing everything without exception,
let us now first discuss what is easy:
I ask you, if a Sage suddenly entered the Hú territory,
would he understand what they say or not?
The challenger will surely say:
‘He knows it.’
As for the principle of knowing it,
how is it demonstrated?
I wish to use your challenge to establish the domain of discernment.
Should he come into contact with them to recognize their words?
Should he blow the pitch-pipes and sound the tubes
to compare their sounds?
Or observe their vital energy and gather their expressions
to know their minds?
If this is knowing the mind
through the vital energy and expressions themselves,
even if they do not speak,
he would still know it.
This way of knowing
can be done without waiting for words.
If he blows the pitch-pipes and compares the sounds
to know their minds:
Suppose the mind is set on a horse,
but one mistakenly says ‘deer’;
the observer would then naturally have to know ‘horse’ through ‘deer’.
This means the mind is not tied to what is said,
and speech may not be sufficient to prove the mind.
If one must come into contact to know the speech,
this is like a child learning to speak from a teacher;
only after that is it known,
so what is so valuable about being perceptive and intelligent then?
Speech is not a thing that is naturally fixed;
the five regions have different customs,
giving different names to the same things,
and they quickly raise a single name
merely as a marker.
A Sage investigates principles to the end,
saying that nature can be traced,
and there is nothing subtle he does not illuminate.
If principles are obscured, then even what is near cannot be seen;
therefore, the speech of foreign lands
cannot be forcibly understood.
Extending this further,
is Gě Lú’s not knowing the cow’s lowing
not perfectly sound?
You also challenged, saying:
Shī Kuàng blew the pitch-pipes
and knew that the southern wind was not competitive
and that Chǔ had many sounds of death.
This is also what I doubt.
May I ask, when Shī Kuàng blew the pitch-pipes,
was it the wind of the State of Chǔ?
They were a thousand lǐ apart,
and the sound would not be enough to reach him.
If he truly recognized the wind of Chǔ
coming into the pitch-pipes,
then to the south of Chǔ are Wú and Yuè,
and to the north are Liáng and Sòng;
if one does not see its source,
how can one recognize it?
Whenever the yīn and yáng are agitated,
only then is wind formed;
when the qì moves in response,
it breaks forth upon touching the ground.
How could it break forth in the court of Chǔ
and come to enter Jìn?
Furthermore, the pitch-pipes merely divide the qì of the four seasons;
when the season arrives, the qì moves;
the pipes respond and the ash shifts.
These all naturally correspond to each other
and do not rely on humans to be functional.
Producing the next notes through rising and falling
is how the harmony of the five tones is equalized
and the divisions of hard and soft are ordered.
However, the pitch-pipes have fixed sounds;
even if one blows the Zhōnglǚ pipe in winter,
its sound remains full and undiminished.
Now, using the qì of a person from Jìn
to blow a pitch-pipe that has no rhyme,
how could the wind of Chǔ come to enter it
and cause it to expand or contract?
Wind has no form,
and sound does not communicate with the pitch-pipes.
Thus, in the realm of comparative logic,
there is nothing to be gained from winds and pitch-pipes;
is it not so?
Perhaps only Shī Kuàng was broadly knowledgeable and well-versed in things,
and naturally had a way to know the signs of victory and defeat,
but wishing to strengthen the people’s hearts,
he attributed it to the divine and subtle—
just as Bó Chángqiān promised longevity to Duke Jǐng.
You also challenged, saying:
the mother of the Yángshé clan heard a child’s cry
and judged that it would ruin the family.
Again, I ask: how did she know this?
Was it that her divine mind had a unique realization,
and her dark words happened to be correct?
Or was it that she had heard children cry before,
and if it was loud and unpleasant like this,
that the current crying sound
was similar to those past crying sounds?
Therefore, did she know it would ruin the family?
If it was a divine mind with a unique realization
and her dark words were correct,
then it was not something obtained through logic.
Even if it is called ‘listening to the cry,’
there was no actual verification found in the child’s voice.
If one takes the sounds previously heard to be unpleasant,
and therefore knows the current cry must be unpleasant,
then this is taking Sound A as the measure
to compare it with the cry of Sound B.
Now, the relation of voice to sound
is like the relation of form to the mind.
There are cases where forms are the same but emotions differ,
or appearances are different but minds are the same.
How is this demonstrated?
Sages have uniform minds and equal virtue,
yet their physical shapes are different.
If minds are the same but forms are different,
then how can one speak of observing the form to know the mind?
Moreover, the mouth’s agitating of qì makes sound;
how is it different from pipes and flutes receiving qì and sounding?
Whether the sound of a cry is good or bad
does not depend on the fortune or misfortune of the child’s mouth,
just as whether the zithers’ tones are clear or muddy
does not depend on the skill or clumsiness of the player.
A mind may be able to discern principles and be good at speaking,
but cannot make the internal flute tuned and smooth;
just as a blind musician may be good at the melody and measure
but cannot ensure the instrument is clear and harmonious.
An instrument does not become fine because of a marvelous blind musician,
and a flute does not become tuned because of a wise mind.
This being so, the mind and the sound
are clearly two separate things.
Since they are indeed two separate things,
then one who seeks the emotions should not linger on observing appearances,
and one who gauges the mind should not borrow from listening to sounds.
For an observer to want to know the mind through sound—
is that not wide of the mark?
Now the mother from Jìn did not get her knowledge from experience or wisdom,
but solely trusted the sound of yesterday
to prove the cry of today.
Is it not that she by chance hit upon the truth, and those of previous generations who loved the marvelous
followed her and praised it?”
The Guest from Qín challenged, saying:
“I have heard that the defeated are not ashamed to flee,
for that is how they stay whole.
My mind is not yet satisfied,
and though my words are challenged,
I will return to follow what remains.
Now, when a calm and peaceful person
listens to the zither, flute, or lute,
their form becomes restless and their will becomes excited.
When they hear the sounds of the qín and sè zithers,
their hearing becomes quiet and their mind becomes leisure.
Within the same instrument,
the melodies used are always different,
and the emotions change accordingly.
Playing the sounds of Qín causes sighing admiration and vehement emotion;
arranging the sounds of Qí and Chǔ makes the emotions unified and the thoughts focused;
indulging in seductive tunes makes one joyful, abandoned, and satisfied in desire.
The mind changes because of the sound,
in ways as numerous as these.
If restlessness and quietude come from sound,
then why limit its sorrow or joy?
Yet you only say that the sound of ultimate harmony
leaves nothing unmoved,
attributing great unity to sound,
while attributing the many changes to human emotions.
Is it possible you know the former but do not understand the latter?”
The Zhǔrén replied:
"The challenge says:
The pípá, zhēng, and dí
make people restless and agitated.
It also says:
Musical compositions differ in their application,
and emotions change accordingly.
This indeed is what makes people constantly affected.
The pípá, zhēng, and dí
have tight intervals and high pitches,
with many variations and frequent rhythms.
Using high pitches to govern frequent rhythms
therefore causes
a person's body to be restless and their will to be agitated,
just as bells and clappers alert the ears,
and bells and drums startle the heart.
Thus, hearing the sound of drums and gongs,
one thinks of generals and ministers;
because sounds vary in magnitude,
their impact on people varies between ferocity and stillness.
The structure of the qín and sè
is leisurely and distant with low pitches,
variations are sparse and the sound is clear.
Using low pitches to govern sparse variations,
if one does not empty the mind and listen quietly,
one will not fully reach the ultimate of clarity and harmony;
therefore, the hearing is quiet and the mind is leisurely.
The different applications of compositions
are just like the sounds of different instruments.
The songs of Qí and Chǔ are often repetitive,
so the emotion is unified;
the variations are subtle,
so the thoughts are focused.
The sounds of beautiful performances
draw upon the beauty of many sounds
and gather the harmony of the five tones.
Their substance is abundant and their application broad,
so the mind is occupied by many principles.
When the five tones gather,
one is joyous and unrestrained, and desires are satisfied.
However, they all take simplicity, complexity, high pitch, low pitch, goodness, and badness as their substance,
while human emotions respond with restlessness, stillness, focus, or dispersion.
It is like wandering through the markets of a capital,
where the eyes are overwhelmed and emotions are unrestrained;
or staying to examine a melody's measure,
where thoughts are quiet and the demeanor is upright.
This is the substance of sound,
which is exhausted in leisure or speed;
the response of emotion to sound
also stops at restlessness or stillness.
Musical compositions differ in their application,
and the way emotion resides in variation
is like flavors having different beauties,
which the mouth immediately recognizes.
The five flavors have ten thousand differences,
but they are largely the same in being delicious;
although musical variations are many,
they are also largely the same in being harmonious.
Beauty has sweetness,
and harmony has joy;
but the emotion following a composition
ends within the realm of harmony;
the mouth responding to beauty
stops at the boundary of sweetness.
How can there be sorrow or joy within them?
However, human emotions differ;
according to what is understood by the master,
it expresses what is held within.
If one says peace, harmony, sorrow, and joy are all equal,
then there is nothing to express first,
and in the end, one attains restlessness or stillness.
If something is expressed,
then it is because there is a master within,
and it is not because of peace and harmony.
Speaking from this,
restlessness and stillness
are the effects of sound;
sorrow and joy
are the masters of emotion;
one cannot see that sound has a response of restlessness or stillness
and therefore say that sorrow and joy both originate from sound.
Moreover, although sounds have ferocity or stillness,
ferocity and stillness each have a harmony,
and that which is moved by harmony
never fails to express itself.
How is this made clear?
When guests fill the hall
and the qín is played when they are merry with wine,
some are delighted and joyful,
while some are miserable and weep.
It is not that sorrow is introduced to the latter
or joy is led to the former.
The sound has not changed from before,
yet joy and grief are both manifested.
Is this not the 'blowing of the ten thousand things being different'?
If there is no master of anger or delight,
then there should be no master of sorrow or joy,
so joy and grief are both seen.
If one relies on a biased and fixed sound,
containing a single consistent tone,
what it illuminates will each match its portion.
Then how could it simultaneously govern all principles
and collectively express all emotions?
From this it is said:
sound takes peace and harmony as its substance,
but its effect on things is not constant;
the mind's intent takes what it awaits as its master,
and it is expressed in response to being moved.
Therefore, sound and the mind
follow different paths and different tracks,
they do not weave together.
How can one dye Tàihé with joy and grief,
or attach empty names to sorrow and joy?"
The guest from Qín challenged him, saying:
"The argument says:
Sounds of ferocity and stillness
each have a harmony,
and that which is moved by harmony
never fails to express itself.
Therefore, when the qín is played when merry with wine,
joy and grief are both manifested.
This means biased and combined emotions
were first accumulated within,
so those holding joy encounter sad sounds and express them,
and those with internal grief meet joyful sounds and are moved.
Sound naturally has a fixed sorrow or joy,
but the transformation by sound is slow and gradual;
it cannot be sudden,
and it cannot immediately change.
Biased and heavy emotions
are triggered when they touch objects,
thus causing sorrow and joy to respond at the same time.
Although both emotions appear together,
how does this diminish the fact that sound has fixed principles?"
The Zhǔrén replied:
"The challenge says:
Sorrow and joy naturally have fixed sounds,
but biased and heavy emotions
cannot be suddenly shifted,
so those holding grief encounter joyful sounds and feel sorrow.
If it were as you say,
and sound had fixed portions,
suppose the Lùmíng was played repeatedly—
this is a joyful sound—
and those with grief encountered it;
although the transformation by sound is slow,
it should only be unable to change them into joy,
how could it further cause them to be sorrowful?
It is like a single flicker of fire:
although it cannot warm a whole room,
it should not increase its coldness.
Fire is not an object of extreme cold,
and joy is not a tool for increasing sorrow.
When the strings are played in the high hall
and joy and grief are both manifested,
it is simply that the harmony releases what is stagnant and guides the emotions,
thereby allowing what is moved by external objects
to express itself fully.
The challenge says:
Biased and heavy emotions
are triggered when they touch objects,
thus causing sorrow and joy to respond at the same time.
Now, regarding those who speak of sorrow,
some see a stool or a staff and weep,
or see a carriage or robes and feel sad.
It is simply because they are moved by the person being gone while the objects remain,
the painful event being manifest while the form is hidden.
The reason they meet these emotions
all have their own causes;
it is not that sorrow is born from touching the ground
or tears flow because one is at a seat.
Now, without a stool or staff to cause the feeling in the listener,
if they shed tears upon hearing harmonious sounds,
is this not because they are moved by harmony
and everything expresses itself?"
The Qín Guest challenged:
"The treatise says:
playing the qín when mellow with wine,
joy and sorrow are both employed.
Wishing to explain these words,
you answered by referring to partial emotions,
which are simply triggered by external objects.
Now, let us speak from the heart
and clarify this through actual effects.
In the human heart, if there is no joy, then there is sorrow;
if there is no sorrow, then there is joy.
This is the broad realm of emotions and intentions.
Yet, weeping is the manifestation of the hurt of sorrow,
and laughing is the function of joy.
I have heard that those who listen to the melodies of Qí and Chǔ
only see countenances of sorrow and weeping,
and never see the appearance of laughing and joking.
This must be because the melodies of Qí and Chǔ take sorrow as their substance;
thus, what they evoke
all corresponds to their measure.
Is it merely because they are heavy and lack variation
that they lead to singular emotion and concentrated thought?
If they truly can cause weeping,
then the fact that sounds possess sorrow and joy
can certainly be known."
The Host replied:
"Although human emotions are moved to sorrow or joy,
sorrow and joy each have their degrees.
Furthermore, the extremes of sorrow and joy
do not necessarily manifest in the same way.
Minor sorrow causes the face to lose composure;
great grief leads to weeping—
this is the way of sorrow.
Minor joy makes the face pleasant;
supreme happiness makes the heart content—
this is the principle of joy.
How can this be clarified?
When one's closest kin are safe and at ease,
then one is as tranquil as if it were natural;
this is what one finds in oneself.
When they are in a crisis
and are only then saved,
then one claps but does not reach the point of dancing.
Speaking from this,
that dancing is not as joyful as the previous state of self-contentment,
is it not so?
As for laughing and joking,
though they arise from joyful feelings,
they are nevertheless formed by external reasons;
they are not the natural instruments for responding to sounds.
In this way, the response of joy to sounds
takes self-contentment as primary;
sorrow's response to stimulation
takes the shedding of tears as its manifestation.
Shedding tears involve physical movement and can be perceived;
self-contentment involves the union of the spirit and has no outward change.
Therefore, one observes the differences
but does not recognize the commonality;
one distinguishes the external
but has not yet examined the internal.
Thus, that laughing and joking are not manifest in sounds—
is it only the melodies of Qí and Chǔ?
Now, if one does not seek joy in the realm of self-contentment,
but because of the absence of laughter claims that Qí and Chǔ embody sorrow,
is it not that one knows sorrow but does not recognize joy?"
The Qín Guest asked:
"Zhòngní said:
'To transform the customs and change the habits,
nothing is better than music.'
If it is as you have argued,
that all forms of sorrow and joy
are not within the sounds;
then the transformation of customs and habits
is actually achieved by what?
Furthermore, the ancients were cautious of decadent trends
and suppressed sounds that indulge the ears;
therefore it was said:
'Banish the sounds of Zhèng,
and distance oneself from flatterers.'
That being the case, then regarding the sounds of Zhèng and Wèi,
or the striking of the sounding stones to harmonize spirits and men,
I venture to ask about the nature of the Zhèng and Yǎ music,
the extremes of their flourishing and decline;
by what means is the transformation of customs and habits achieved?
I hope to hear about this again
to resolve my doubts."
The master replied to him, saying:
"As for the saying that 'transforming customs and changing habits'
must follow a period of decline and corruption.
The kings of antiquity,
receiving the Mandate of Heaven to govern all things,
necessarily exalted the teachings of simplicity and ease
and managed through the governance of non-action (Wúwéi).
The ruler was tranquil above,
and the ministers were compliant below;
the profound transformation communicated latently,
and Heaven and man reached a state of harmonious intersection.
Even withered and dried things
were gradually nurtured by spiritual fluids;
within the six directions (Liùhé),
all bathed in the vast current [of virtue],
washing away dust and grime.
All living beings enjoyed ease and leisure,
seeking much happiness for themselves;
silently they followed the Dào,
cherishing loyalty and embracing righteousness,
without even being aware of why it was so.
A harmonious heart was sufficient within,
and harmonious energy (héqì) appeared without.
Therefore, they sang to express their intent
and danced to proclaim their feelings.
Afterward, they embellished it with colorful patterns,
illuminated it with the Fēng and Yǎ,
broadcast it with the eight musical sounds (Bāyīn),
and moved it with the Supreme Harmony (Tàihé),
guiding their spiritual energy,
nurturing it until it was complete.
Welcoming their nature and emotions,
they brought them forth and made them clear;
making the heart and principle conform to each other,
and the energy and sound correspond to each other,
merging into a thorough understanding
so as to accomplish its beauty.
Thus, the sentiment of joyful music
is manifested in bells and chimes;
its magnanimity and glory
are revealed in the tones and sounds.
In the past, the ten thousand states shared the same customs;
their fragrant flourishing was together abundant,
as fragrant as autumn orchids.
Trust was established without expectation,
and success was achieved without scheming.
Solemnly they loved one another,
like unfolding brocade and spreading colors,
brilliant and magnificent to behold.
The prosperity of the Great Way (Dàdào)
was never more magnificent than this;
the achievement of Great Peace (Tàipíng)
was never more manifest than here.
Therefore it is said:
'For transforming customs and changing habits,
nothing is better than music (Yuè).'
As for the substance of music,
the heart is primary.
Therefore, soundless music
is the parent of the people.
When the Bāyīn harmonize,
that which people delight in
is also collectively called music.
However, the transformation of customs
does not fundamentally lie in this.
For when tones and sounds are in harmony,
it is something human emotions cannot cease to seek.
Thus the ancients knew that emotions cannot be unleashed,
so they restrained their tendencies toward evasion;
they knew that desires cannot be extinguished,
so they guided them from their source.
They created rituals (Lǐ) that could be upheld
and established music (Yuè) that could guide.
The mouth did not exhaust all flavors,
and music did not go to the extremes of sound.
They calculated the appropriateness of beginnings and ends
and measured the middle ground between the wise and the foolish;
they made regulations for it,
causing the distant and near to share the same customs.
Though used, it was never exhausted;
it was also used to bind loyalty and trust
and to manifest constancy.
Thus, village schools and local academies followed this as well,
causing string and bamboo instruments to exist alongside sacrificial vessels,
feather-dances and ritual shields to be used along with bows and yielding,
and correct words to be uttered together with harmonious sounds.
This ensured that when one was about to listen to these sounds,
one necessarily heard these words;
when one was about to observe these appearances,
one necessarily honored these rituals.
Rituals are like the rising and descending of hosts and guests;
only then is the exchange of toasts performed.
Thus, the moderation of speech,
the measure of sounds,
the etiquette of bows and yielding,
and the frequency of movement and stillness,
with advancing and retreating needing each other,
together formed a single body.
Rulers and ministers used it at court;
the various scholars used it at home.
Practicing it in youth
and not growing negligent in adulthood,
their hearts were at peace and their wills were firm.
Moving toward goodness day by day,
then they approached it with reverence
and maintained it for a long time without changing;
only then was transformation completed.
This was the intention of the former kings in using music.
Therefore, at court banquets, diplomatic visits, and sacrificial offerings,
auspicious music must be present.
Thus, national historians collected the prosperity and decline of customs,
entrusting them to music masters
and proclaiming them through pipes and strings.
This allowed those who spoke to be without blame,
and those who heard to be sufficiently self-warned.
This was also the intention of the former kings in using music.
As for the sounds of Zhèng (Zhèngshēng),
they are the most exquisite of tones and sounds.
Exquisite sounds move people
just as beautiful colors confuse the will.
To be addicted to pleasure and wild with wine
makes it easy to lose one's livelihood.
Unless one is an Ultimate Person (Zhìrén),
who can resist it?
The former kings feared the world would drift away and not return,
so they prepared the Bāyīn,
but did not profane the sounds.
They brought the Tàihé to a limit
and did not exhaust its variations.
They reduced seductive sounds,
making music joyful but not licentious,
just as the Great Soup (Dàgēng) is unseasoned,
not exhausting the flavors of the ladle and herbs.
If the flow is shallow and near,
then the sound is insufficient to please
nor is it something to be enjoyed.
If those above lose their way
and the state loses its discipline,
then men and women chase after each other,
becoming licentious and wild without measure.
Then customs change because of this,
and habits are formed by what is liked.
If they esteem what their will is set upon,
then the crowds will indulge in it.
If they delight in what they are accustomed to,
then how can they be punished?
By relying on harmonious sounds,
pairing them and prolonging them,
sincerity is moved by words
and the heart is affected by harmony.
Once customs are established,
they are named accordingly.
However, the sounds so named
do not inherently contain licentiousness or evil.
Whether they are licentious or correct is the same as what is in the heart.
The substance of the Yǎ and the Zhèng
is also sufficient to observe."
One essay of the Shì Sī Lùn.
As for those called *Jūnzǐ*,
their minds do not dwell on right and wrong,
and their actions do not deviate from the *Dào*.
Why is this said?
Those whose *qì* is calm and spirit is empty
do not harbor vanity or ostentation in their minds;
those whose nature is clear and minds are far-reaching
do not tie their emotions to what they desire.
Since vanity and ostentation do not exist in the mind,
they can transcend *Míngjiào* and follow *Zìrán*;
since emotions are not tied to desires,
they can discern between high and low status and understand the nature of things.
When the nature of things is followed and understood,
there is no deviation from the *Dàdào*;
by transcending names and following the heart,
right and wrong find no place to dwell.
Therefore, when speaking of the *Jūnzǐ*,
not dwelling on things is the primary principle,
and understanding all things is considered beauty.
When speaking of the *Xiǎorén*,
concealing their feelings is considered a fault,
and deviating from the *Dào* is seen as a deficiency.
Why is this?
Concealing feelings and being boastful or stingy
are the ultimate evils of the *Xiǎorén*;
an empty mind and not dwelling on things
are the sincere practices of the *Jūnzǐ*.
Thus, speaking of the *Dàdào*,
"If I had no body,
what calamity would I have?"
Regarding the lack of high regard for life as precious
is superior to valuing life.
From this perspective,
the mind of the *Zhìrén*
certainly does not harbor any dwelling.
Therefore, *Yī Yǐn* did not grudge being worthier than *Yīn Tāng*,
so the age was saved and his name became illustrious.
*Zhōu Dàn* ignored suspicion and acted in private,
so by acting as regent, the transformation of the people flourished.
*Yíwú* did not hide his feelings from *Qí Huán*,
so the state became a hegemon and the ruler was honored.
In their use of the mind,
how could they have been tied to private interests for their own sake?
Thus *Guǎn Zǐ* said:
"When the *Jūnzǐ* practices the *Dào*,
he forgets his own person."
These words are true.
When the *Jūnzǐ* acts worthily,
he does not examine whether there are rules before acting.
He follows his heart without deviousness,
not deliberating on what is good before being upright.
He displays his feelings without dwelling on them,
not discussing what is right before doing it.
Thus, by loftily forgetting his worthiness,
worthiness and rules meet;
by spontaneously following his heart,
the heart and goodness encounter each other;
by freely not dwelling on things,
affairs and rightness go together.
Therefore, regarding the discussion of public and private:
even if one says they aim for the *Dào* and preserve goodness,
◇ and have no wickedness,
if there is nothing they harbor that they do not hide,
they cannot be called selfless.
Even if they have the desire to boast of goodness
or their feelings deviate from the *Dào*,
if there is nothing they hold that they do not reveal,
they cannot be called unpublic.
Now, by holding to the principle of absolute publicness
to regulate unpublic feelings,
it causes those who do good
not to be separate from having private interests;
and though they may desire to boast of goodness,
they do not fall into being unpublic.
By valuing their reputation and prizing their mind,
then the feelings of right and wrong
cannot help but be revealed.
When right and wrong are necessarily revealed,
those who have goodness will not have the wrongness of hiding feelings,
and those who have faults will not add the great fault of being unpublic.
If there is no "not right," then goodness is always attained;
if there is no great fault, then their faults will not be excessive;
this is how to rescue them from their faults.
It is not only to perfect goodness,
but also to encourage those who are not good.
Goodness is used to perfect goodness,
and faults are used to rescue from faults,
how much more so with the extremes of right and wrong.
Therefore, goodness and lack of goodness
are the ultimate nature of things.
If one stands between these two things,
wherever one goes,
one will surely succeed through publicness and fail through privateness.
Using the same vessel,
yet there is success and failure.
Publicness and privateness
are the paths of success and failure,
and the gates of fortune and calamity.
Thus, those who are extreme in nature but do not change are few;
those who are not extreme but are in practical use are many.
If one has the substance of an average person,
and operates with the quality of practical use,
yet rests the heart upon ancient heroes
and treads upon the public path, speaking from the heart—
then there will be nothing wrong in one's words;
if one acts by following one's feelings,
then in affairs there will be nothing but good fortune.
Thus, what others dwell upon
is not what one dwells upon.
What desires take as private
is not what one takes as private.
If words encounter goodness without calculating gain or loss,
and actions encounter fortune without being measured against right and wrong,
is this not the principle of public success and private failure?
If it is like this,
then what dwelling is there?
Thus *Lǐ Fú* revealed the theft;
*Jìn Wén* was joyful and easygoing;
*Bó Dī* cried out his crime,
so loyalty was established and his life was preserved.
*Miù Xián* confessed his fault,
his words were accepted and his reputation praised;
*Jiàn Lí* spoke his sincerity,
and the whole hall shed tears.
Yet these several men all faced the calamity of losing their lives
and stood at an unpredictable moment,
but by revealing their minds and consciousness,
they still attained safety.
How much more so for a *Jūnzǐ* who does not have the crimes of those men,
but has their goodness?
Dwelling on the feeling of being good
is what is problematic.
Only by seeing a problem as a problem
does one not have the problem;
to have a problem but be able to cure it
is also superior to just having the problem.
However, there are also affairs that seem wrong but are not wrong,
and those that resemble what is right but are not right;
these must be examined.
Therefore, in the mechanism of flexibility and change,
there may be pride that leads to yielding,
greed that leads to integrity,
foolishness that results in wisdom,
or endurance that aids benevolence.
However, at the time of pride or stinginess,
one cannot say there is no integrity;
in the appearance of suspicion or endurance,
one cannot say there is no benevolence.
This is what seems wrong but is not wrong.
Or slanderous words may seem trustworthy,
yet one cannot say there is sincerity;
inciting a thief may seem like loyalty,
yet one cannot say there is no selfishness.
This is what resembles what is right but is not right.
Therefore, one must discuss the use of their mind,
determine where they are heading,
hold to their words to measure their principles,
and examine their feelings to find their changes,
observing where they begin
and naming where they end.
Then the feelings of those acting privately
will not be able to allow their wrongs by relying on what seems wrong;
the minds of those who are pure and bright
will not be forced to betray their rightness by treading on what seems right.
Thus, what is truly right is revealed after a temporary appearance of being wrong,
and what is truly wrong is clarified after a temporary appearance of being right.
When public and private are both revealed,
then those who act privately have nothing to hope for,
and those who are pure and bright have nothing to be disappointed by.
When those who act privately have nothing to hope for,
