they will think of correcting their wrongs;
when those who stand for the public have nothing to fear,
they will act without doubt.
This is the way of great governance.
Thus the mistress spilled the sweet wine
and was executed for her crime;
*Wáng Líng* argued in court,
while *Chén Píng* followed the ruler's will.
Looking at it from this,
are these not cases of what seems wrong but is not wrong?
To clarify the sincere practice of the *Jūnzǐ*,
and reveal where public and private lie,
those filling the hall and the steps
all see it
and say:
"A good person."
However, those who turn their backs and withdraw to discuss while harboring private interests
are no longer the same.
Those who hold ◇ and hide their feelings without changing,
truly their spirits are lost in what deludes them,
and their bodies are drowned in conventional fame.
Their minds are controlled by what they fear,
and their feelings are tied to what they desire.
All of them think they are in the right,
and that no one is worthier than themselves.
Not yet having suffered the pain of flesh-rending
or the calamity of a shocked heart,
they are ultimately unable to withdraw their feelings to reflect on themselves,
or to discard fame to follow reality.
Thus in their hearts they hold this as right,
One hides it for selfish reasons;
even if the intention contains goodness,
the artifice of it makes it evil.
Failing to manage what should be managed,
yet managing what should not be managed;
not seeking the principle of why one does not act,
but seeking the way of how to act.
Therefore, while they are clear about artifice,
they are ignorant of the act itself;
thus they regard non-action as clumsy
and consider meticulous artifice as skillful.
They only fear their concealment is not subtle,
and only worry their hiding is not secret.
Thus they have an air of pride and defiance
to display to common people;
they use affected speech
to solicit popular reputation.
They claim these are excellent rules for eternal years,
and that nothing is more magnificent than this;
galloping their thoughts all day long,
they never peek outside of it.
Thus they can form a system for their selfishness,
but they lose their natural essence.
Consequently, the disposition for concealment
will certainly reside in their hearts;
the machinations of falsehood and negligence
will certainly manifest in their affairs.
If it is like this,
then the discussions of right and wrong are already clear,
and the reality of rewards and punishments is firm.
They do not know that staying in the shade can eliminate shadows,
but instead worry that the shadow is not hidden;
they do not know that non-artifice can eliminate troubles,
but instead worry about the failure of their artifice—is this not lamentable!
Thus Shēn Hóu complied improperly
and was rejected by Chǔ Gōng;
Zǎi Pǐ indulged in selfishness
and ultimately suffered disaster.
Speaking from this,
there has never been one who embraced concealment and looked to self-interest
and yet established himself in a pure world;
nor one who hid faults and concealed emotions
and yet had their trustworthiness and reputation become prominent.
Since a Jūnzǐ possesses the right essence
and also observes these mirrors,
he values honesty and understanding,
spreading and preserving them;
he loathes pride and stinginess,
discarding and distancing himself from them.
If he commits a single wrong in his artifice,
he feels ashamed before his spirit within;
if he hides a single deficiency out of lowliness,
he feels ashamed of his form without.
His speech has no improper taboos,
and his conduct has no improper concealment.
He does not call something good just because he loves it,
nor does he call something wrong just because he hates it.
His heart has nothing to boast of,
and his emotions have no attachments;
his body is pure and his spirit is upright,
so his sense of right and wrong is appropriate.
His loyalty moves the bright Tiānzǐ,
and his trustworthiness is firm among the myriad people.
He places his mind in the eight desolations,
demonstrating magnanimity throughout all his days.
Is this not the beauty and excellence of the high conduct
of a sage or a Jūnzǐ?
Someone asked:
"Did Dìwǔ Lún have selfish desires?"
The answer was:
"In the past, when my brother's son was ill,
I went ten times in one night to visit him, yet returned and slept peacefully.
When my own son was ill,
I did not go to see him all morning,
yet I could not sleep all through the night.
Can such a case be called selfish?
Or is it not selfish?"
The reply said:
"This is a fault,
but it is not selfishness.
Selfishness is characterized by not speaking out,
while public-spiritedness is characterized by speaking fully.
Goodness has no stinginess as its substance,
and faults are a burden because of intentional artifice.
Now Dìwǔ Lún reveals his feelings,
this is being without selfishness;
to be concerned with the visits and the lack of sleep,
this is having a fault.
One who is without selfishness yet has faults
has a mind without artifice.
Those who speak of having no artifice
are not required to be perfect in everything;
those who speak of many attachments
are simply not complete in their silence.
Therefore, many attachments lead to faults,
while lack of artifice leads to correctness.
However, the reason why lack of artifice has correctness
is because the will has nothing it values above all,
the heart has no desires,
it reaches the essence of the Great Way,
and acts according to nature;
then there is no path leading to faults.
Embracing Oneness and having no artifice,
then one is without selfishness.
To be without faults and possess both meanings
is indeed the ultimate beauty.
If one has faults but can speak of them,
this is more virtuous than the selfishness of not speaking;
it is not that having no feelings is the greatest of faults.
Now Dìwǔ Lún has faults but can reveal them,
so he cannot be called not public-spirited.
What is revealed as right and wrong
cannot be called having artifice.
To call having a fault 'selfish'
cannot be called anything but confusion.
This is the principle of public and private."
One Discourse on Guǎn and Cài
Someone asked:
"According to the records,
Guǎn and Cài spread rumors
and rebelled against the Eastern Capital.
Zhōu Gōng conducted a punitive expedition,
and executed them for their heinous treason;
their stubborn wickedness was prominent,
and their names have flowed down for a thousand years.
Moreover, their enlightened father and sage brother
could not perceive their wickedness and foolishness in their youth,
nor notice their lack of virtue as family members,
but instead sent them to govern the chaotic and weary people of Yīn,
granting them honorable ranks in the vassal states,
allowing their evil to accumulate and their crimes to be completed,
until they finally met with calamity.
This is logically inconsistent,
and my mind cannot find peace with it.
The answer was:
"Excellent is your question.
In the past, Wén Wáng and Wǔ Wáng employed Guǎn and Cài based on their substance;
Zhōu Gōng executed Guǎn and Cài based on expediency.
The matters of expediency are manifest,
while the principles of their substance are submerged.
Therefore, the people of the time entirely regarded Guǎn and Cài as stubborn and malevolent;
now I shall discuss this for you.
Guǎn and Cài both submitted to the teachings and sacrificed themselves for righteousness;
their loyalty and sincerity were natural.
This is why Wén Wáng ranked them and made them prominent,
and the two sages Fā and Dàn
promoted and employed them.
It was not because of personal affection or favoritism;
it was how they honored virtue and respected the worthy,
aided the distressed people of Yīn,
and supported and assisted Wǔ Gēng
to reform stubborn customs.
Their achievements bore fruit,
so they were not discarded for a generation;
their names were foremost at the time,
and they were ranked as vassal ministers.
When it came to the death of Wǔ,
the successor Sòng was young and immature.
Zhōu Gōng took over the administration
and led the feudal lords in court,
seeking to glorify the past records
and exalt the royal enterprise.
But Guǎn and Cài followed the teachings
but did not understand the sage's use of expediency.
Suddenly encountering a great change,
they could not adapt themselves.
Loyal in their hearts,
their thoughts were with the royal house;
thus they raised their voices and led the masses,
wishing to remove the nation's trouble,
to assist and preserve the Son of Heaven,
and willingly seeking to destroy Dàn.
This was a foolish sincerity bursting forth,
which invited disaster upon them.
Chéng Wáng had a great realization,
and Zhōu Gōng manifested restoration,
unifying and rectifying the customs,
and using righteousness to sever affection.
Although internally they were as sincere as their hearts,
externally their standing was not established;
they took up arms in rebellion,
and those they deluded were many.
Therefore, with forbearance, he imposed punishment,
shedding tears while carrying out the execution,
to demonstrate rewards and punishments
and not avoid his own relatives.
The honor and rank displayed
must be concentrated on great virtue;
the execution and lashings applied
must be added to the guilty.
This is the correct form of teaching
and the clear righteousness of ancient and modern times.
Though Guǎn and Cài harbored loyalty and embraced sincerity,
they ultimately met with execution for their crimes.
Once the execution for crimes was manifest,
they could no longer be vindicated.
Their inner selves were necessarily obscured
and their evil deeds consequently made public.
The paths of the obscure and the public are vastly different,
thus for successive generations, they have not been vindicated.
However, commentators follow the name and believe in the deeds,
thus considering Guǎn and Cài as evil,
not knowing that the 'evil' of Guǎn and Cài
would imply that the three sages were not enlightened.
If the three sages were not unenlightened,
then a sage would not bless evil nor employ the stubborn and malevolent.
Since the stubborn and malevolent have no place in an enlightened age,
then Guǎn and Cài received no favoritism from their father or brothers;
their employment was necessarily due to their loyalty and goodness,
so the two uncles were originally virtuous and good.
Now if we trace back to the three sages' use of enlightenment to reveal merit,
grant them the principles of their substance,
and infer that the loyal and worthy may be ignorant of expediency,
while discussing the great principles of governing a state,
then the goodness of the two uncles becomes manifest,
the employment by the three sages had its reasons,
the cause of the rumors had its origin,
and Zhōu Gōng's execution was correct.
Furthermore, when Zhōu Gōng acted as regent,
Shào Gōng was displeased.
Inferring from this,
that Guǎn and Cài harbored doubts
does not mean they were not worthy;
the loyal and worthy may not grasp expediency.
The three sages did not employ the wicked,
yet Zhōu Gōng had no choice but to execute them.
In this way,
those the three sages employed were indeed good,
Zhōu Gōng's execution was appropriate,
and the hearts of Guǎn and Cài are understood.
Then the great righteousness can prevail,
both internal and external matters are ordered,
without contradicting or betraying one another,
and the contemporary discourse can be clearly and greatly resolved."
A Treatise on Insight and Courage
There was a certain Lǚ Zǐ
who refined the meaning and savored the Dào,
investigating the truth of right and wrong;
he believed that a person may have courage without insight,
but if one has insight, one will have courage.
Jī Xiānsheng believed that insight and courage have different uses
and cannot produce each other.
The treatise says:
"The original qì molds and smelts,
and all living beings receive from it.
There are variations in the amount received,
thus talent and nature have darkness and light.
Only the Perfect Man uniquely concentrates pure beauty,
encompassing both the external and internal,
lacking in nothing.
Below this,
things are generally deficient.
Some are insightful in seeing things,
some are brave in making decisions.
Human dispositions range from greedy to upright,
each stopping at their own limit;
like plants and trees,
they are classified and distinguished.
Those who possess both are broad in things;
those who receive only part keep their portion.
Therefore, I say insight and courage are different breaths
and cannot produce each other.
Insight is for seeing things;
courage is for making decisions.
Having only insight without courage,
then though one sees, one does not decide.
Having only courage without insight,
then one violates reason and loses the opportunity.
Thus Zǐjiā was weak
and fell into the crime of assassinating his ruler;
Zuǒshī could not decide
and was pressured by Huá Chén.
Both had wisdom that reached the matter but lacked the decision to act.
This principle is clear,
yet not without doubts or obstacles.
Therefore, I have briefly raised one corner,
hoping that doubts will not recur."
Lǚ Zǐ said:
“I have respectfully read your recent discourse;
it may be said that even the vastness of the sea could not add anything to it.
In analyzing principles, one prizes conciseness while exhausting the essence;
why uphold superficialities and rambling absurdities?
Now, your argument
actually draws upon the Húnyuán as an analogy;
how remote and sprawling it is!
Therefore, I shall respond directly with the urgent essentials of human affairs.
Jiǎ Shēng of the Hàn dynasty
presented policies of blunt directness
and exerted the height of perilous words.
His acting without hesitation
was due to the clarity of his perception.
When he loathed the fú and wrote the fù,
he was clouded by confusion.
Can the courage of a single person
truly have expansion and contraction?
It is because of seeing or not seeing
that action is either fruitful or not.
Zǐjiā and the Zuǒshī
were all foolish, confused, shallow, and flawed;
their clarity was not penetrating.
Thus they were confused by ambiguity
and ultimately met with disaster.
Could one have clear perception and illumination yet lack decisiveness in courage?
Thus, Huò Guāng possessed a spirit of profound bravery
and held the office of Great General,
yet he trembled during the matter of Wáng Hè.
Tián Yánnián was a man of letters
who never had a martial reputation,
yet he stated his righteousness and spoke with vigor;
his courageous spirit reached the clouds.
Is this not proof?
As for Yúqī offering his head
and the mother of Wáng Líng falling on her sword,
cases of those who were clear and resolute
are of ten thousand kinds like these;
if one wished to record them in detail,
they would be beyond words.
How much more so for those who see a level path but dare not set foot on it,
or who ascend the cloudy road but hesitate upon reaching the Tàiqīng?
If the foolish and flawed sorts have ability,
they entrust themselves to the midst of dark ambiguity
and cast their bodies into pitfalls,
like Dào Zhí hiding his body within the tiger’s jaws,
or a thief putting his head first into a ditch;
as for attacking a tiger with bare hands and crossing a river without a boat,
such kinds of foolish daring
can indeed exist.
This is why I say that clarity does not possess courage;
without courage, one can still maintain a partial stance.
This easily understood principle
does not require many analogies.
Therefore, I do not draw distantly upon tedious words.
If you have not yet inferred the other three corners from the one shown
and still have doubts,
I hope to receive your later instructions
to further display my arguments.”
“In discussing the principles of nature and disposition,
and analyzing differences and similarities,
one should naturally seek the beginning and end of what is received
and deduce the origins of the distribution of *qì*.
Only by following the source to the end
will one not be in contradiction.
Now you wish to discard the Húnyuán
and pick up only what is seen;
this is liking the mesh of a net
but hating to hold the main cord.
The original argument was that the two *qì* are not the same,
and clarity does not produce courage.
If one wishes to argue this to the end,
one should take a person who is utterly devoid of courageous gall
but possesses the clarity to perceive affairs.
Therefore, there should be the harm of not being resolute.
It is not that the blood and *qì* of an average person
disappear and then return;
if provided with clarity,
and the two *qì* exist within one body,
then clarity can direct courage;
Jiǎ Yì is an example of this.
Jiǎ Yì’s clarity and courage
were sufficient to regulate each other,
therefore he could accomplish things.
Who said he had no courage at all
and relied solely on clarity to act?
You alone have created these words
to suit your own argument.
His being confused by the fú
was where his clarity was not comprehensive;
how does that harm his courage?
Once clarity has seen the object,
courage can carry it out.
If clarity does not see,
what should courage decide upon?
They support each other in advancement and retreat;
how can this be called expansion and contraction?
Even if we take your words:
Jiǎ Shēng presenting policies

his loathing the fú and writing the fù

if clarity can advance and retreat,

You say Huò Guāng possessed profound bravery

Jiǎ Shēng’s confusion regarding the fú

Tián Yánnián’s burst of energy,

Tián Yánnián participating in the council

His heroic spirit surging forth

clarity does not have courage,

Based on your words,

As for all your other various examples,

Refutation of the “Discourse on the Natural Love of Learning,” one piece.
As for the nature of the people,
they like safety and hate danger,
and they like ease and hate toil.
Therefore, if they are not disturbed,
then their desires are fulfilled;
if they are not coerced,
then their wills are followed.
In the age of *Hónghuāng*,
the *Dàpǔ* was not yet diminished;
those above had no artificial refinement,
and those below had no competition.
All things were complete and principles were in harmony;
none were not content.
When full, they slept peacefully;
when hungry, they sought food.
Joyfully patting their stomachs,
they did not know they lived in an age of *Zhìdé*.
In such a state,
how could they know the origins of *Rényì*
or the refinements of *Lǐlǜ*?
But when the *Zhìrén* no longer existed
and the *Dàdào* declined,
people began to create writing
to transmit their ideas.
They distinguished between the various things,
causing them to be categorized.
They established *Rényì*
to entangle the heart.
They instituted *Míngfèn*
to regulate external conduct.
They encouraged learning and lectured on literature
to make their teachings seem divine.
Consequently, the *Liù Jīng* became convoluted
and the *Bǎijiā* flourished,
opening the path to glory and profit,
so that people rushed toward them without realizing it.
Thus, just as birds greedy for life
eat the grains of garden ponds,
scholars seeking security
betray their own wills to follow the customs.
Holding pens and tablets,
they find enough to sustain themselves;
accumulating learning and clarifying the classics,
they use this to replace the work of farming.
Therefore, they study because they are in distress,
and they use study to achieve glory;
they practice only after calculating gains,
and their habits are formed by what they favor.
It seems like *Zìrán*,
and thus it makes you call it *Zìrán*.
But if we trace its origin:
the *Liù Jīng* prioritize suppression and guidance,
while human nature finds joy in following its desires.
Suppression and guidance go against one's wishes;
following desires attains *Zìrán*.
Therefore, the attainment of *Zìrán*
does not come from the suppression and guidance of the *Liù Jīng*;
the basis of preserving one's nature
does not require the *Lǐlǜ* that violate one's feelings.
Hence, *Rényì* are devoted to managing the artificial
and are not the essential methods for nourishing the true;
integrity and yielding arise from contention and seizure,
and are not produced by *Zìrán*.
Speaking from this perspective:
birds do not mutilate themselves to seek taming,
and beasts do not group together to seek domestication;
thus, the true nature of humans
has no reason to properly and naturally indulge in this study of ritual.
Your argument also says:
fine meats and rare delicacies,
though never tasted before,
will surely be found delicious upon tasting
because they suit the mouth.
Being in a dark room
and seeing the light of a candle,
one is pleased in the heart without being taught.
How much more so in the darkness of a long night,
when one receives the light of the sun;
one's feelings of depression change,
and one's ignorance is dispelled.
Although things come from the periphery,
feelings respond from the root;
thus there is no harm to the *Zìrán* of loving learning.
My rebuttal says:
the mouth's relation to sweet and bitter,
or the body's relation to pain and itching—
these are movements stimulated by objects
and actions responding to things;
they do not require learning to be capable
and do not wait for external help to exist.
These are inevitable principles
that I do not dispute.
Now you take an inevitable principle
and use it to illustrate the "not necessarily inevitable" love of learning;
I fear this is an argument that seems correct but is false,
and the "learning is like a single grain" theory
resides right here.
Now you establish the *Liù Jīng* as the standard
and look up to *Rényì* as the core,
using rules and regulations as your carriage
and teaching and instruction as your nursing;
if one follows this path, they advance;
if one deviates from this road, they are blocked.
Letting the mind wander and the eyes gaze to the limit,
one still does not see beyond it;
galloping all year round,
one's thoughts do not leave their assigned position.
Gathering with your clan to offer advice,
you hold only learning as noble;
clutching books and picking out sentences,
looking up and down while sighing in admiration,
you make people take these words to heart
and consider them a source of glory.
Thus you call the *Liù Jīng* the sun
and not learning the long night.
But if we were to treat the hall as a servant's quarters,
and see chanting and reciting as the speech of ghosts,
the *Liù Jīng* as overgrown weeds,
and *Rényì* as stinking rot;
if looking at texts made the eyes dim,
practicing bows made the back hunch,
wearing official robes caused cramps,
and discussing ritual texts caused tooth decay;
and if we then discarded them all together
to start anew with all things,
then even if you loved learning without tire,
you would still find it lacking.
Then the previous lack of learning
would not necessarily be a long night,
and the *Liù Jīng* would not necessarily be the sun.
A common saying goes:
"A beggar does not insult a horse doctor."
If one encountered the rule of the unlettered ancients,
one could obtain peace without learning
and achieve one's will without toil;
so what would one seek from the *Liù Jīng*,
or what would one desire from *Rényì*?
Speaking from this,
do not today's scholars
first calculate and then study?
If one acts only after calculating,
then it is not a response of *Zìrán*.
Your talk
is, I fear, like finally developing a taste for calamus pickles.
A rebuttal of "No Good or Bad Fortune in Dwellings" and a Treatise on Nourishing Life.
The spirits and deities are far away,
and good and bad fortune are hard to clarify.
Though an average person exhausts themselves,
they cannot find the source,
and thus are easily misled by the Way.
Therefore, *Fǔzǐ* stopped answering questions about them
and was cautious about spirits and the supernatural, not speaking of them.
Thus the ancients displayed benevolence toward things
but kept its application hidden within themselves;
they knew it could not be shared with the masses.
It was not that they intentionally hid it,
but that it was not something those people could understand.
I have no intention of attaining perfection, but you follow your own heart and narrow views,
being absolutely certain without doubt.
Your commitment is such
that it suffices for your own judgment.
I have reflected on your previous arguments,
and many of their points are logically unsound.
I have respectfully followed your words
to raise this rebuttal.
You are currently deducing the elements of metal and wood,
yet you do not know where they reside,
nor how they manage food.
The world has no principle of self-regulation,
and the law has no technique for solitary goodness.
If it is not the right person,
the Way does not act in vain.
Ritual, music, government, and punishment—
these constant external matters
still have their shortcomings;
how much more so for things that are profound and subtle?
Even if you want to distinguish the divine and subtle,
dispel confusion,
resolve stagnation,
and establish a starting point
to clarify the causes;
even if you judge decisively to regulate the essentials,
only then would there be evidence.
If you only gather the common views of the ignorant,
like silkworm seeds,
and then discard them in anger,
claiming there is no principle of *Yīnyáng* or good and bad fortune,
is that not like choking and then hating grain,
or drowning and then blaming the boat?
The discourse says:
A palace that lasts a hundred years
cannot make a shāngzǐ live long;
the stars of Kuí and Gāng in isolation and opposition
cannot make Péng Zǔ die young.
It also says:
The physiognomy of Xǔ Fù,
and the branding of Tiáo Hóu and Yīng Bù before they became kings,
are all matters of nature and fate.
The response says:
This implies that fate is fixed
and longevity has a set place.
Calamity cannot be escaped with wisdom,
and blessings cannot be attained by force.
Yīng Bù feared pain,
but ultimately suffered the knife and saw.
Yà Fū dreaded starvation,
but in the end, he had the affliction of hunger.
Among all things and all matters,
all that is encountered
is nothing but physiognomy and fate.
However, in the era of Táng and Yú,
why did everyone’s fate extend equally?
Among the soldiers of Chángpíng,
why were all their fates shortened together?
This is what I doubt.
If it were as discussed,
even if one were as cautious as Zēng and Yán,
they could not avoid calamity.
If one were as evil as Jié and Zhì,
they would naturally be prosperous and flourishing.
If auspiciousness and misfortune were fixed from the start
and could not be shifted,
then why did the ancients say: “A family that accumulates goodness
will surely have surplus celebration”?
“Treading in faithfulness and thinking of obedience,
Heaven will bless them”?
It must be that goodness is accumulated before blessings respond,
and faithfulness is manifest before protection arrives,
just as crimes invite punishment
and merit leads to reward.
If one first accumulates and then receives the retribution,
this is what is attained through the principles of matters,
not something encountered by chance in the dark.
If everything is called “physiognomy,”
this would be determining physiognomy and fate based on actions,
and fixing auspiciousness and misfortune based on knowledge and effort;
I fear this is not the intent of the original discourse.
This is another thing I doubt.
It also says:
If one eats much and does not digest,
one must take yellow pills.
If life is naturally destined to continue,
why fear eating much?
And why take good medicine?
If you say taking medicine is part of what physiognomy entails,
then is the dwelling not also part of it?
If you say that although there is fate,
one still must use medicine to save oneself,
how do you know physiognomy does not need a dwelling to assist itself?
If you say medicine can be discussed but the dwelling cannot be spoken of,
I fear there may be some in the world who would speak of it.
You have said that longevity and premature death cannot be sought,
even more so than wealth and status;
yet you also say that those who are good at seeking longevity and strength
must first know the source of disasters and illnesses
before they can be prevented.
If so, can longevity and premature death truly be sought?
Or can they not be sought?
You have said that Péng Zǔ lived seven hundred years
and the premature death of a shāngzǐ
are both the natural results of nature and fate;
yet you also say that not knowing how to prevent illness
leads to longevity departing and premature death arriving.
Seeking reality from emptiness,
thus nature and fate are not fulfilled.
This implies that the arrival of longevity or premature death
arises from how one uses the body,
and the fulfillment of nature and fate
is obtained through skillful seeking.
If so, for those who die young,
how can they not be called foolish?
For those whose lives are extended,
how can they not be called wise?
If longevity and premature death are determined by folly or wisdom,
then as for the discourse on natural fate
that cannot be sought,
where is it to be placed?
In all these several points,
there are contradictions in the refined discourse.
The discourse says:
Concentrating the breath to achieve softness,
having few private interests and few desires,
acting directly according to what is appropriate for one’s nature,
and conforming to the correct standards of nurturing life,
seek it within one’s own embrace,
and you will attain it.
It also says:
Those who are good at nurturing life
consider harmony to be the ultimate.
How true are these words!
It is not that I think otherwise,
but only that preserving life is not exhausted by this.
One does not enter a state in peril
to avoid the harm of chaotic governance.
One doubles the gates and strikes the clapper
to prepare against the disaster of violent madness.
A dwelling must be bright and high
to distance oneself from the affliction of wind and toxins.
All external things that can cause harm
cannot be fully enumerated.
How can maintaining a single harmony be considered the ultimate?
As for concentration, stillness, and few desires,
none were like Shàn Bào, who at seventy years of age
had the complexion of a child;
he could be said to have used softness and harmony.
Yet one morning he was eaten by a tiger;
was this not because he relied on the internal and neglected the external?
If you say Shàn Bào’s physiognomy was destined to supply the kitchen,
and even wisdom could not avoid it,
then what was the benefit of having few desires?
And how can you say nurturing life is attainable?
If Shàn Bào met disaster because he was not perfectly good,
then the way of assisting life
does not stop at a single harmony.
If harmony is not enough to protect life,
then as for external things that cause affliction,
I do not know how they can be equalized.
The discourse says:
If a master divines an existing dwelling, there is proof,
but if they are made to create a new one, there is no evidence.
May I ask: as for divining an existing dwelling and having proof,
is it merely divining the walls and rooms?
Or is it divining the auspiciousness or misfortune of the occupant?
If by divining the occupant one knows of prosperity or decline,
this is divining the person,
not divining the existing dwelling.
If by divining the existing dwelling one knows of auspiciousness or misfortune,
this means the house itself has good or evil,
and the occupant follows it.
Therefore, the diviner observes the external
and attains the internal.
If a house can control a person and make them follow it,
then a person destined for good fortune
would receive disaster in an inauspicious house;
and the wicked and unprincipled
would obtain blessings in an auspicious dwelling.
Is the result of auspiciousness or misfortune
due only to the house?
If it is further caused by the person,
why is there no evidence for a new one?
If auspiciousness or misfortune should indeed come from the person,
then even with an existing dwelling,
how can you say there is proof?
If this is so,
can it actually be divined?
Or can it not be divined?
Does the dwelling actually exist?
Or is there no dwelling?
The essay says:
A dwelling is like divination by tortoise shell or stalks;
it can be used to know good or bad fortune,
but it cannot cause good or bad fortune.
The response says:
These are similar but not the same.
In divination, good and bad fortune are not predetermined;
one waits for things to happen and then responds;
it is a sign of the future.
When judging a dwelling, one does not ask whether the resident is wise or foolish,
but only observes what has already come to be.
What is passed down
is a form already completed.
It is like seeing a dragon-like countenance
and knowing someone will be noble,
or seeing vertical lines on the palm
and knowing someone will starve.
Each has a cause for being so;
it is not based on ignorance.
Now, seeing that they are the same in terms of obtaining knowledge of good or bad fortune,
people therefore say judging a dwelling
is no different from divination;
this is like seeing a *qín* and calling it a *kōnghóu*;
it is not only that they do not know the *qín*.
Even if it were as the essay states,
that a dwelling and divination are the same,
in that they can only know but not cause fortune,
then if good and bad fortune are already fixed,
what is the use of knowing?
Whether one divines or not
makes no difference at all.
Yet when the ancients were about to act,
they always said that they must ask the tortoise and stalks if it is auspicious,
to determine where the error might lie;
how could this be in vain?
This is again where my doubt lies.
When *Wǔ Wáng* established the *Zhōu*,
it was said he examined the divination,
and the dwelling was to be in *Hào Jīng*.
When *Zhōu Gōng* moved the city,
he then divined at the *Jiàn* and *Chán* rivers,
and ultimately determined to reside at *Luò*.
It is also said:
Divine for the dwelling and tomb and then settle there.
The ancients practiced this;
in the past, it was thus.
You negate it;
today, it is like this.
I do not know whose determination should be followed.
The essay says:
Even if a dwelling is made for the *Sāngōng*,
foolish people will certainly not become *Sāngōng*;
this is clear.
Some say:
Foolish people will certainly not be able to live long in the dwelling of a duke or marquis.
If so, then is there really no such thing as the influence of a dwelling?
The response says:
I do not say an auspicious dwelling
can produce blessings on its own;
I only say that when a *Jūnzǐ* already possesses talent and wisdom,
and also divines his residence,
follows the right path and accumulates virtue,
he then enjoys great fortune.
It is like a good farmer who already possesses fine skills,
and also chooses fertile soil,
and then adds weeding and hilling;
only then does he have the reward of a full granary.
Now, seeing that foolish people cannot obtain blessings from an auspicious residence,
you then say dwellings have no good or bad qualities.
How is this different from seeing that a field produces no harvest
and saying the field has no distinction between fertile and barren?
Although a fine field is beautiful,
the crops do not flourish on their own;
although a divined dwelling is auspicious,
success is not achieved on its own.
The principle of mutual dependence is truly thus,
and so the good and bad fortune of a dwelling
cannot be doubted.
Now, if one trusts only in omens,
one abandons what is appropriate to human principles;
if one adheres only to divination and physiognomy,
one cuts off the good and bad fortune of *Yīn* and *Yáng*;
if one relies only on knowledge and strength,
one forgets where the *Tiāndào* resides.
How is this different from knowing that timely rain makes things grow,
and therefore folding one's arms and waiting for fine grain?
For this reason, theories of doubt and wonder arise,
and debates of partial correctness flourish.
Their foundations are not unified;
how can they communicate with each other?
As for those who combine and excel in both,
would they not be half wrong about graves and dwellings?
The essay says:
Calamities caused by times and days
did not exist under the great kings of antiquity;
they were favored by the kings of declining ages.
These words sound good,
but look closer, they are not entirely so.
*Tāng* prayed in the *Sānglín*,
and *Zhōu Gōng* held the jade tablet;
I do not know if these were for calamities or not.
"The auspicious day is *Wù*,"
"Having prayed to the ancestor of horses and offered prayers";
I do not know if these concern times and days or not.
These are all matters of your own school,
established by former masters,
yet you turn your back on them in a single morning.
If *Tāng* and *Zhōu* were not great kings,
I hope you will examine this again.
Furthermore, comparing these two worthies,
how do they compare to you?
The essay says:
When bandits are about to arrive,
making a swift escape is the priority;
when food does not digest,
taking yellow pills is the first step.
You only know that this is better than a moment's safety
or begging from a barbarian,
but you do not know how to suppress bandits and illness before they take shape,
so that the work is profound and without failure.
Rescuing someone from fire with water,
though one may pride oneself more than the one carrying firewood,
one does not know the priority of curving the chimney.
Moreover, regarding the subtle matters of the world,
words cannot reach them,
and calculations cannot distinguish them.
Therefore, the ancients left them as they were without debating them,
understood them through spiritual clarity,
and thus knew future things.
Thus, they could observe alone before the myriad transformations
and reap success after great compliance.
The common people call it *zìrán*,
but they do not know why it is so.
In such a case,
how could common logic reach it?
Now, even for things with clear forms and numbers,
you are still stuck on them;
Heaven and Earth are vast and far-reaching,
and the varieties of things are many; what wisdom knows
is not as much as what is unknown.
Now, you hold onto the technique of *bìgǔ*,
saying that the cultivation of life is already complete
and the ultimate principle has been exhausted.
Letting your mind race to the limit of observation,
you stop here and return;
what your thoughts cannot reach,
you say does not exist.
You wish to rely on what you see
to determine what was difficult for the ancients to speak of;
would this not be like a *huìgū* discussing ice?
You wish to use what you know
to... discard what...
would this not be like a *Róng* person asking about cloth in the *Zhōngguó*,
seeing the hemp seeds and then not cultivating them?
I am hesitant to make arbitrary judgments;
moving forward, I dare not fix misfortune or fortune on divination and physiognomy,
and moving backward, I dare not say that a household has no good or bad fortune.
Response to the Difficulties in "Dwellings Have No Good or Bad Fortune" from the "Treatise on Preserving Life."
The *Xiānwáng* handed down instructions,
to establish regulations for average people;
these are what are established through words.
The wise and the foolish do not deviate from them;
they are that from which affairs originate.
Unchanging from the past to the present,
they are the means by which teaching is achieved.
As for the mysterious and subtle mechanism of the spirit,
and the transformation that occurs without words,
unless one is of the utmost essence,
who can participate in it?
Therefore, those who are good at seeking
observe things in their subtlety
and extend their knowledge by analogy,
without using themselves as the measure.
According to the argument presented,
to hold that things "excessively exist" is folly,
and to hold that they "extremely do not exist" is absurd.
Now, if one posits "slight existence,"
does that then avoid folly?
And can "complete non-existence" avoid absurdity?
If "slight existence" is not folly,
I do not know where the limit of "slight existence" ends.
If "complete non-existence" can avoid absurdity,
then as for "extreme non-existence,"
there is no reason to call it absurd.
It is also said:
when private spirits are established,
then public spirits are discarded.
Thus, it is only a dislike for the harm the private does to the public
and the injury the heterodox does to the orthodox,
rather than a claim that there are no spirits.
Previously, *Mòzǐ* established the reality of public spirits,
a theory characterized as "not excessive existence";
while causing *Dǒng Shēng* to rely on the path of correct prohibitions,
holding to the words "not extreme non-existence."
Can the elegant aims of these two worthies
be joined into one,
so that neither is lost?
What is being debated now
is the desire to seek actual existence and actual non-existence
to clarify that nature is not deceptive;
arguments have skill or clumsiness,
and discussions on teaching have refinement or coarseness.
Seeking the intent of your elegant discourse,
you claim the *Hé* and *Luò* are not sincere
but borrow from spirits and ghosts;
thus you consider ancestral temples
to be means of spiritualizing their origin.
By not answering *Zǐgòng*
in order to seek the truth of it,
do you, sir, not rely in your heart on the non-existence of spirits and ghosts,
aligning yourself with *Dǒng Shēng*?
Yet you look back at the words of the ancients,
fearing the harm of having no spirits and ghosts;
with appearance and essence diverging,
you establish a discourse of discarding the private for the public,
wishing to bridge the two extremes
so as to be neither foolish nor absurd,
criticizing both *Dǒng* and *Mò*.
Do you think that middle ground
can be occupied?
I fear that although the rhetoric is clever,
it is difficult for both to be consistent.
This is also not what is expected of a rigorous discourse.
Therefore, I say the ancients aligned their virtue with *Tiāndì*,
and their actions responded to nature;
of what they established to govern the world,
none was without evidence.
Would they covertly set up ancestral temples to trick their descendants?
Or vainly borrow spirits and ghosts to deceive the future?
You might say I am no different from *Mò*;
now I do not deny agreeing that ghosts exist,
but I do not stubbornly hold to one side;
I clarify what is as it should be,
making humans and ghosts consult together,
and the dark and the light help each other.
This is also the way to seek the mean,
and this is where I differ.
The discourse states:
Sages and commoners are equal in illness,
yet their prayers are not the same.
Therefore, regarding a minister or a younger brother,
Zhōu Gōng prayed for their lives;
but regarding his own person,
Ní Fù did not pray.
This is what is meant by ritual being the outward appearance of emotion.
The objection says:
If it concerns a minister or a son,
then it is appropriate to cultivate the appearance of emotion.
Yet one has not heard of Shùn or Yǔ praying for their ruler or father.
If regarding one's own person it is not done,
then one has not heard of Wǔ Wáng having a command to stop prayers.
When Tāng prayed at Sāng Lín,
was he again acting for a ruler or father?
Inferring from this,
if prayer is considered beneficial,
then Tāng and the Zhōu kings used it;
if prayer has no effect,
then Kǒng Zǐ would not have requested it.
These are different paths leading to the same goal,
following the significance of the times.
It also says:
Auspicious times and days were what the former kings used to warn against negligence
and to encourage the handling of affairs.
Your previous discourse said:
Auspicious times and days were not something the Sage Kings possessed;
therefore, I asked about the matter of Wéiwù.
Now you do not answer whether Wéiwù is actually right or wrong,

trace the beginning and investigate the clues;

when one does get prey,

resulting in one not daring to lift a foot,
sitting and guarding what is rootless?

to explore the profound and search for the hidden,

Admonition of the *Tài Shī*
Vast and boundless was the Great Prime (Tàisù),
when the Yáng shone and the Yīn congealed.
The Two Poles (Èryí) molded and transformed,
and human relations first arose.
In the beginning, all was dim and obscure;
there was no calculation and no striving.
Desire opened the way for material things,
and trouble was born from human affairs.
Risking danger and encountering harm,
wisdom could not save life.
To honor a leader and return to benevolence (rén),
is a natural sentiment.
Therefore, the way of the sovereign is natural;
it must rely on the worthy and the brilliant.
Vast and hazy in the past,
there was none who was not at peace.
After Hèxū had passed,
Huángxī succeeded him.
Silent and still, without formal records,
the Great Simplicity (Dàpǔ) was not yet diminished.
All things were harmonious and joyful,
neither dying young nor being separated.
Coming to the time of Táng and Yú,
they still earnestly maintained that legacy.
Their character was based on ease and simplicity,
responding to Heaven and following the rules.
They wore robes of coarse cloth
and lived in dwellings of earth and wood.
If any thing lost its nature,
they feared as if the fault were their own.
Consulting widely to brighten their accomplishments,
they ultimately abdicated to Shùn and Yǔ.
He who governs is burdened with labor,
while those who look up to him are at ease.
The Perfect Man (Zhìrén) values his person;
he discards power without regret.
Thus Zǐzhōu claimed illness,
and the man of Shíhù took to a raft;
Xǔ Yóu bowed low
and declined the leadership of the Nine Provinces (Jiǔzhōu).
The former kings practiced benevolence and love,
pitying the world and grieving for the times;
lamenting that all things were about to fall into ruin,
only then did they take charge.
Coming down to the decline of virtue,
the Great Way (Dàdào) sank into oblivion.
Cleverness and cunning were used daily,
and people gradually favored their own kin.
Fearing that things would drift apart,
they bared their arms to establish benevolence (rén).
Profit and ingenuity were increasingly contested,
and complex rituals were repeatedly displayed.
Punishments and doctrines vied for application,
destroying nature and losing truth.
In the later ages of decline,
heirs inherited the foundation.
Relying on status and depending on power,
they treated none as friends or teachers.
Carving up the world
to serve their own private ends.
Thus the sovereign’s position became more extravagant,
and the ministers began to harbor ulterior motives.
They exhausted their wits in plotting for the state,
not sparing themselves even unto ashes.
Although rewards and punishments remained,
they neither encouraged nor restrained.
If one is arrogant and full of himself, giving rein to his will,
obstructing with troops and usurping power;
boasting of majesty and indulging in cruelty,
disasters will pile up like hills and mountains.
Punishments were originally meant to chastise the violent,
but now they are used to threaten the worthy.
Formerly, rule was for the sake of the world;
now, it is for the sake of one person.
Those below hate those above,
and the sovereign suspects his ministers.
Death and disorder become widespread,
and the state then falls into ruin.
Thus Yīn Xīn was unprincipled,
and his head was hung from a white banner;
the Zhōu court failed in its standards,
and the people of Zhì plotted.
Chǔ Líng was extremely violent,
and his forces collapsed at Gānxī;
Jìn Lì was cruel and oppressive,
and Luán Shū created trouble.
Zhǔfù abandoned ritual
and died like a starving chick;
Qín Huáng inflicted misery and poison,
and disaster flowed across the Four Seas (Sìhǎi).
Consequently, fallen states follow one after another,
succeeding each other from ancient times to the present.
They loathe destruction,
yet they follow the signs of their own demise.
Secure as a mountain at first,
but later collapsing in ruin.
Facing the blade and the sharp point,
what can regret add then?
Therefore, let those who dwell as emperors and kings
not say, "I am honorable,"
while neglecting their virtuous reputation;
let them not say, "I am strong,"
while indulging in pride and excess.
Discard those fawning favorites,
and accept these blunt countenances.
Flattering words are pleasant to the ear,
but they stain virtue and breed disaster.
To the long-lasting common people,
I direct my appeal.
Grant office only to the worthy;
why must they be relatives?
If you follow and create what is good,
the people will indeed follow your example.
As for the source of order and chaos,
are there no flourishing teachings?
The majestic Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ)
meditates on his faults.
With an open mind, he guides the people,
sincerely seeking upright words.
As a minister and teacher in charge of instruction,
I venture to offer this before him.
Family Admonitions (Jiā Jiè)
A man without a will
is not a man.
But when a Jūnzǐ applies his mind,
that which he desires to carry out
must be appropriate.
Gauging what is good,
he must deliberate and only then act.
If the will is directed toward something,
then the mouth and heart swear an oath
to hold onto it until death without wavering.
Feeling ashamed if his conduct falls short,
he aims for certain success.
If the mind is weary and the body slack,
or if one is pulled by external things,
or burdened by internal desires;
if one cannot endure immediate troubles
or suppress small emotions,
then one deliberates whether to persist or quit.
When deliberating whether to persist or quit,
then two minds struggle with each other.
When two minds struggle,
then the emotions that previously enslaved one will prevail.
Some abandon their path halfway,
and some fail when they are but one basket of earth short of completion.
Using such a mind to hold fast, one is not firm;
using it to attack, one is weak.
Swearing an oath with it, there are many violations;
planning with it, secrets are easily leaked.
In times of pleasure, one indulges one's feelings;
in times of leisure, one gives full rein to one's whims.
Therefore, although there is a flourish of brilliance,
there is no merit of producing fruit;
despite a year of toil,
there is not a single day's achievement.
This is why the Jūnzǐ sighs.
As for the long chanting of Shēn Xū,
the complete purity of Yí and Qí,
the adherence to faith of Zhǎn Jì,
and the maintenance of integrity by Sū Wǔ,
these may be called firm.
Therefore, holding to it with the tranquility of a mind without distractions
and embodying it
as if it were natural,
is the height of maintaining one's will.
Regarding the local officials where you reside,
you should simply respect them and nothing more;
you should not be extremely intimate,
nor should you visit frequently;
visits should occur at proper times.
When there is a crowd,
you should not remain alone behind others,
nor should you stay overnight.
The reason for this is
that officials like to ask about outside matters;
if they occasionally take action based on this,
then those who are resentful will say it was because of what you said,
and you will have no way to clear yourself.
If you act broadly and speak little,
and are cautious and self-contained,
then the path of resentment and blame will be dissolved.
One's conduct should be pure and aloof.
If there are troublesome or humiliating requests,
wanting someone to give their life
or asking someone to seek favors,
one should decline with humble words;
state that you habitually do not involve yourself in such matters,
and they should understand.
If there is a grievance or emergency
that your heart cannot bear,
you may outwardly decline
while secretly helping them.
The reason for this is
that above, it keeps you far from the machinations of compliance;
in the middle, it cuts off the requests of common and licentious people;
and below, it preserves the reputation of an unblemished character;
this is also one aspect of holding to one's will.
Whenever doing something, first examine its feasibility;
if it is appropriate,
and this thing should be done,
yet others wish to change it,
you should explain the reason why it should be changed.
If the other person's words are truly superior,
do not be ashamed to yield or persist in error;
if their logic is insufficient
and they instead use emotions to press their request,
then even if they talk on and on,
you must firmly hold to your position;
this is also one aspect of holding to one's will.
There is no need to practice the trivial spirit of minor integrity;
if you see the destitute
and have the means to provide relief,
then act upon seeing what is right.
If someone has a request of you,
first reflect and consider;
if it involves great loss
but the righteousness of the relief provided today is small,
then you should weigh the importance and refuse them.
Even if they continue to beg or insult you without ceasing,
you must still cut them off.
However, in general, when people make requests,
it is because they lack what I have,
so they come to ask me;
this is considered giving much.
If it is not so,
and you exhaust yourself for trivial things,
unable to speak frankly to their face
and forcing yourself to satisfy a small emotion,
that is not having will.
As for speech,
it is the mechanism of the Jūnzǐ;
when the mechanism moves, things respond,
and the forms of right and wrong become manifest.
Therefore, one cannot but be cautious.
If you do not fully understand a matter
but your original intention was to speak,
then you should fear the mistake of lack of understanding
and temporarily restrain yourself.
Looking back later, if not speaking of the matter
caused no harm,
then speaking earlier might have been harmful;
thus, being able to not speak
allows one to maintain everything correctly.
Furthermore, common people spread good news slowly and bad news quickly,
and they like to discuss the faults and shortcomings of others;
this is the talk of ordinary people.
What is said in social gatherings,
unless it is a high-minded discussion,
but merely gossip about activities and news,
or minor differences of opinion,
you should simply look past it;
it is not worth answering.
Do not speak unless it is righteous;
being thorough, quiet, and respecting the Dào,
is this not what is meant by "few regrets"?
If people are arguing with each other
and the outcome is not yet known,
be careful not to get involved.
Simply observe in silence;
the right and wrong will naturally become apparent.
Some small right is not worth affirming,
and some small wrong is not worth refuting;
in the end, one can simply not speak and wait.
Even if someone asks,
you should still decline by saying you do not understand.
Recent debates are also like this.
If at a wine gathering
you see people arguing,
and the situation seems to be escalating,
you should leave immediately for no reason.
This is a sign of an impending fight.
Watching from the side, you will surely see who is right and who is wrong;
being partial, you cannot help but say something.
If you speak, you must side with one person;
the one who is not right
will still consider himself to be in the right,
and will think that the person who called him wrong is biased toward the other,
and thus feelings of resentment and hatred will arise.
Or you might receive insulting words;
by watching,
you see much right and wrong,
and if the argument is not resolved,
then being benevolent without being forceful
serves no purpose for righteousness;
therefore, you should stay away.
However, generally, those who argue
are merely petty people.
Even if there is right and wrong,
they are all wallowing in the same mess together;
even if one wins, is it worth praising?
If you cannot stay away, getting drunk is better.
If you happen to have something you wish to keep secret
and the other person insists on knowing it,
if they keep begging without end
or use vulgar emotions to coerce you,
do not be afraid of these petty people
and be pulled in by them.
They try to lead you to exhaust your words.
Now, firmly saying
you do not know or do not recognize it
is what it means to have will.
Unless they are old friends or neighbors,
for those of lower status
who wish to invite you,
you should decline with another reason
and not go.
If you view glory as external, you will have few desires;
unless it is extremely urgent,
never making requests of others
is the highest beauty.
There is no need to perform minor acts of humility;
one should be grandly modest and generous.
There is no need to perform minor acts of integrity;
one should maintain grand yielding.
Like yielding an office when attending court,
or yielding one's life when facing righteousness—
as when Kǒng Wénjǔ asked to die in place of his brother—
this is the integrity of loyal ministers and heroic men.
Every person has their own public and private matters;
be careful not to force yourself to know what others know.
If they know that I know it...
then they will be suspicious of me.
Now if I know but do not speak,
then it is as if I do not know.
If you see people whispering in private,
you should leave and rise up immediately,
do not let them be suspicious of you.
Sometimes they may press you,
and force you to talk with them.
If their words are deviant or treacherous,
then you should assume a serious expression and correct them with morality and righteousness.
Why is this?
Because a Jūnzǐ does not tolerate false or shallow speech.
Once the matter fails,
they will say that "Mǒu Jiǎ previously knew about my affairs,"
and therefore they will take deep precautions against you.
In the private talk of ordinary people,
there is nothing they will not say;
you should be mindful of this beforehand.
As for those who run away upon seeing it,
why is that?
Perhaps they happened to learn of some private matter;
if they agree with them it is fine,
but if they do not agree, the others fear the matter will leak,
and think of harming the person to erase the traces.
If someone you do not admire
comes to play or joke,
or mocks the flaws of others,
simply do not respond and move from small association
to eventually having no association;
but do not be overly cold or arrogant,
and quickly answer them with silence.
Since the situation cannot last,
they will stop on their own.
Unless it is someone you supervise,
and there is no other reason for mutual adjustment,
if there is an intention of sharing wine or food,
or the courtesy of a small gift,
this is what human relations permit,
so there is no need to refuse.
Beyond this,
unless you are deeply intimate,
gifts of silk
or the presentation of carriages and clothing
should be strictly rejected.
Why is this?
Ordinary people all value righteousness lightly and value profit heavily;
if they exhaust themselves to give now,
they must be acting for a purpose or selling a favor,
using goods to seek favor and demanding a reward.
This is what common people desire,
but what a Jūnzǐ greatly detests.
...... further confused,
there is no need to pester others
or forcefully urge people to drink wine.
If they do not drink, let it be;
if someone comes to urge you,
you should always take it for them,
neither mocking nor refusing.
When you see you are slightly tipsy, then stop;
be careful not to reach a state of extreme drunkenness,
where you cannot control yourself.
Four-character Poem
Drifting, drifting, the white clouds,
turn according to the wind;
Deep, deep, the green waters,
fill the hollows and descend.
Riding the current to a distant departure,
I personally go to the orchid cove.
Leaning on a staff to answer them,
I receive it in my simple heart.
Long whistling on the clear plains,
I only use it to express my sorrow.
Far, far flies the Luán,
spreading its wings in the Great Clarity;
Looking down at the Purple Star,
looking up at the Plain Court.
Treading upon the dark void,
floating and sinking without form.
About to travel beyond the world,
I whistle for my companions with a long cry.
If the spirit... does not remain,
with whom shall I travel alone?
There is a boat floating and capsizing,
bound by ropes and cables.
With oars of juniper and paddles of pine,
it is like a dragon's subtlety.
...crossing the ford through danger,
traversing the crossing and not returning.
Thinking of friends in the vast forest,
embracing simplicity at the mountain's brow.
Guarding the vessel and sacrificing for one's work,
one cannot fly away.
Becoming an immortal at Mount Huà,
soaring above the clear sky.
The cloud canopy moves softly,
the six dragons flutter.
On the left, wearing pepper and cassia,
on the right, adorned with orchid sprigs.
Lìng Yáng praises the road,
Wángzǐ attends the carriage.
Beautiful is the famous mountain,
where the Perfected Man is to be met.
Leveling all things and nourishing life,
wandering freely with the Dào.
Three Five-character Poems
Human life is like the morning dew,
the world's changes are full of many traps.
If there must be a final end,
then Péng and Dān are not worth much.
Benevolence and righteousness water down pure simplicity,
foreknowledge loses the flower of the Dào.
Clinging to weakness loses naturalness,
the heavenly truth is difficult to harmonize.
The man of Yǐng scrutinized Jiàng Shí,
Zhōng Zǐ recognized Bó Yá;
Perfected Men do not often exist,
who shall harmonize with a high song?
In the long night the house is at peace,
I walk alone by the side of the bright courtyard.
Raising my head to look at the heavenly path,
the flowing light shines upon the eight extremities.
Touching my heart, I mourn this degenerate age,
and remotely think of the Great Dào being constrained.
Fluttering are the men in power,
leisurely they advance through their own difficulties.
Gain and loss come from oneself,
glory and disgrace eat away at each other.
Though vermilion and purple are like black and yellow,
Tài Sù prizes being without color.
Deep and placid, embodying the Ultimate Dào,
the transformation of colors is like the flow of breath.
Common people are not to be befriended,
Sōng and Qiáo are those to be neighbors with.
Why stay amidst the filth and turbidity,
where every movement adds to the grime and dust?
Resolute, I go on a distant journey,
preparing my carriage to wait for a propitious time.
Lightly rising to soar beyond the world,
washing my wings at the Fú Sāng ford.
Wandering and playing on the spirit peaks,
playing the zither and chanting of the Great Truth.
The dark waters wash my five organs,
my transformation is sudden as if a god.
Héng É offers the wondrous medicine,
my feathers and plumage shine with new light.
With one leap I reach Kāi Yáng,
and look down upon the men in power.
Alas, the people of this world,
how can they be worthy of long-term reliance?
Poem on Roaming as an Immortal
Fluttering is the phoenix-linchpin,
encountering this net.
From Tàipíng Guǎngjì volume 400, citing Xù Qíxié Jì.
Rhapsody on Wine
Heavily brewed wine is most clear,
like a deep pool or congealed ice.
It possesses all nourishing fluids,
fragrant and transparent.
From Běitáng Shūchāo volume 148.
Encomium on the Zither
Beautiful is my elegant instrument,
its raw material came from the spirit mountain.
Its form possesses virtuous truth,
pure, harmonious, and natural.
Washed as if by spring snow,
placid as a cavern spring.
Gentle is its benevolence,
with the luster of jade and outward freshness.
Formerly in the time of Huáng Nóng,
the divine object arrived.
August was Zhòng Huá,
who entrusted his heart to the five strings.
It stilled evil and admitted the upright,
tirelessly and transcendentally.
Spreading harmony and nourishing Qì,
it grants long life.
From Běitáng Shūchāo volume 109.
